coi_statement: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Feedback learning is thought to involve the dopamine system and its projection sites in the basal ganglia and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), regions associated with procedural learning. Under certain conditions, such as when feedback is delayed, feedback‐locked activation is pronounced in the medial temporal lobe (MTL), which is associated with declarative learning. In event‐related potential research, the feedback‐related negativity (FRN) has been linked to immediate feedback processing, while the N170, possibly reflecting MTL activity, has been related to delayed feedback processing. In the current study, we performed an exploratory investigation on the relation between N170 and FRN amplitude and memory performance in a test for declarative memory (free recall), also exploring the role of feedback delay. To this end, we adapted a paradigm in which participants learned associations between non‐objects and non‐words with either immediate or delayed feedback, and added a subsequent free recall test. We indeed found that N170, but not FRN amplitudes, depended on later free recall performance, with smaller amplitudes for later remembered non‐words. In an additional analysis with memory performance as dependent variable, the N170, but not the FRN amplitude predicted free recall, modulated by feedback timing and valence. This finding shows that the N170 reflects an important process during feedback processing, possibly related to expectations and their violation, but is distinct from the process reflected by the FRN.</jats:p>

A multi-institutional, prospective, observational study was conducted, involving 15 medical oncology departments in Spain, where medical oncologists manage patients eligible for palliativeintent systemic anticancer treatment. This work is part of the NEOetic cancer patient research program funded by the Bioethics Group of the Spanish Society of Medical Oncology (SEOM). All eligible cases were identified and included consecutively by oncologists. Subjects were informed that their participation was voluntary, anonymous, and confidential. Informed written consent was obtained from all prior to data collection. Inclusion criteria required participants to be over 18 years of age and to have a histologically confirmed diagnosis of locally advanced, unresectable, or metastatic cancer qualifying for systemic treatment with palliative intent. Individuals with any serious mental illness that would prevent them from comprehending the survey were excluded. Data collection procedures were consistent across all hospitals and data were collected and updated by the medical oncologist, through a webbased platform (www.neoetic.es).

Approval was granted by the Ethics Committee of Michigan State University (#STUDY00008501). || FundingThe authors disclosed receipt of the following financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article: This research was supported in part by the Dr. Delia Koo Global Faculty Endowment from the Asian Studies Center at Michigan State University. || Grant: STUDY00008501 || Korean immigrant mothers of children with disabilitiesIn the USA, Korean immigrant mothers of children with disabilities encounter unique challenges. Language and cultural barriers can make it especially difficult to access special education services (Cho et al., 2000(Cho et al., , 2003;;Jegatheesan, 2009;Kim et al., 2021;Park et al., 2001). Mothers may not understand the English terminology or procedures involved. They may also struggle to find and work with educators, therapists, psychologists, medical providers, and lawyers (Cho et al., 2000(Cho et al., , 2003;;Lee & Park, 2016;Park et al., 2001). Moreover, they frequently face stigma and discrimination associated with their children's disabilities, race, and ethnicity (Cho & Gannotti, 2005;Lee et al., 2022;Park et al., 2001). Many Korean immigrant mothers may hesitate to confront school personnel when their children have not received appropriate educational services (Cho & Gannotti, 2005;Jegatheesan, 2009;Park et al., 2001). This reluctance can be attributed to their intersecting identities as both immigrants and women, and the fear of reprisals for their children (Cho & Gannotti, 2005;Jegatheesan, 2009;Kim & Kim, 2017;Park et al., 2001).However, Korean immigrant mothers in the USA have demonstrated remarkable resilience and resourcefulness by finding ways to navigate the complex educational system and protect the rights of their children (Kim & Kim, 2017;Kim et al., 2007). Kim and Kim (2017) reported that these mothers embrace their role as advocates and researchers beyond their traditional parental responsibilities. For example, some parents enhance their understanding of disability-related services and their rights through formal programs provided by professional organizations (Cho & Gannotti, 2005;Kim et al., 2007;Lee & Park, 2016). Others have connected with the Korean community to access information about available services, such as attending support groups or obtaining information from a Korean nonprofit for people with disabilities (Cho & Gannotti, 2005;Kim et al., 2007;Kwon et al., 2023). In some cases, mothers have taken legal action, such as refusing to sign special education documents due to unsatisfactory plans and progress, hiring an advocate, or requesting a due-process hearing (Cho & Gannotti, 2005).The deficit view of mothers of children with disabilities often depicts them as trapped by numerous challenges and with limited agency to advocate for their children (Burke & Goldman, 2018;Lasky & Karge, 2011). However, to provide effective and culturally relevant support, it is important to adopt a strength-based approach and recognize the different methods, approaches, and actions that immigrant mothers employ to promote their children's educational achievement and wellbeing (Kim & Kim, 2017).

funding_statement: CONCLUSIONDespite some limitations, the present results from a large community sample and based on bifactor analysis offer additional support for the presence of a general VDT factor at the core of borderline pathology, vulnerable narcissism, and (although less so) Factor 2 psychopathy, which was hypothesized in a previous investigation by Miller et al. (2010) based on nomological network analysis. The VDT model was confirmed using both EFA and CFA, and in separate analyses for men and women subsamples, with validity indices suggesting that factors were strong and reliable. The proposed model is coherent with other established conceptualizations of personality pathology (e.g., HiTOP; Kotov et al., 2017). Results regarding borderline pathology provides support to previous findings (e.g., Sharp et al., 2015) suggesting that its distinctive clinical features might represent the main core of personality disorders. Our findings also highlight some meaningful distinctions between borderline pathology and vulnerable narcissism, and add to previous findings (Miller et al., 2010) that Factor 2 psychopathy is probably the less representative member of the VDT.This research was supported by a grant from the R eseau de Bio-Imagerie du Qu ebec/Fonds de recherche du Qu ebec -Sant e: R eseaux de recherche th ematiques awarded to SH, DG, and VMC. funding_statement: AmeriCorps Office of Research and Evaluation (ORE), Grant/Award Number: 18REHOH001 || Grant: 18REHOH001 || | CARE Cincinnati's refugee and immigrant civic leadership programThe goal of CARE Cincinnati's Refugee and Immigrant Civic Leadership Program was to facilitate a CBPR process where the CARE team would develop and enact their agenda for empowered civic engagement in Cincinnati (Dutt et al., 2022a;Jacquez et al., 2021). The CARE team developed the program which consisted of five workshops: (a) an introduction to Cincinnati government, (b) community organizing (how to work with others in your community to work for change), (c) narrative advocacy and public speaking (how to tell your story to policy makers and stakeholders), (d) equity and inclusion in civic work (how to be an advocate for justice for everyone), and (e) group reflection and strategizing. Workshops were held every other Friday evening via the video calling software Zoom (due to COVID-19 pandemic precautions needed in 2021) and generally included a guest speaker and discussion.Workshops were conducted largely in English with live interpretation provided for all participant language needs. Each participant was provided with a welcome package of fact sheets about Cincinnati, the aggregated data collected from previous CARE team surveys, and a small gift bag of CARE memorabilia. coi_statement: Declaration of Conflicting InterestsThe author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interests with respect to the authorship and/or publication of this article. || Keywords sexual assault, reporting/disclosure, adult victims, interventionSexual assault is a widespread social issue with a profound impact on survivors' physical, mental, and emotional health (Campbell et al., 2009;Jina & Thomas, 2013). While anyone can be victimized, it is disproportionately perpetrated by men against women and gender diverse individuals (Planty et al., 2013;Wirtz et al., 2020). Nationally representative studies have found that approximately one in five women have experienced a completed or attempted rape, and 46% of women have experienced some type of unwanted sexual contact during their lifetimes (Smith et al., 2018). Survivors 1 are often advised to seek out a medical forensic exam (MFE) after an assault, which includes medical evaluation and treatment as well as forensic evidence collection (Department of Justice, 2013). The forensic evidence and related documentation are placed in a sexual assault evidence kit (SAEK), which can be released to police for DNA testing and to aid in investigation and prosecution of the assault (Zweig et al., 2014(Zweig et al., , 2021)).However, sexual assault survivors have historically been treated poorly by the criminal legal system (Shaw et al., 2017;Tillman et al., 2010), and many express reservations about reporting their assaults. Quantitative analyses comparing case characteristics of reported versus nonreported assaults have found that survivors are more likely to report when their assault reflects stereotypical characteristics of rape, such as an unknown assailant, physical force, and victim injury; conversely, survivors are generally less likely to report their assaults when the assailant is known to the victim or when the victim was assaulted while incapacitated due to drugs or alcohol (Ceelen et al., 2019;Wolitzky-Taylor, 2011).Qualitative research has expanded on these findings, indicating that survivors often do not report their assaults because they do not want others to know about the assault, want to handle it themselves, fear retaliation, fear being blamed or disbelieved by police, lawyers, or others involved in the criminal legal system, do not know if the incident was serious enough to report, or blame themselves for the assault (Ceelen et al., 2019;Cohn et al., 2013;Lorenz et al., 2021;Zinzow & Thompson, 2011). Cohn et al. (2013) distilled these reasons further with a principal component analysis that identified a three-factor solution: others knowing (i.e., not wanting family or others to know), nonacknowledgment (i.e., not knowing if it was serious, harmful, or criminal enough to report), and criminal justice concerns (i.e., concerns that reporting would lead to nonfavorable outcomes). These results are largely congruent with the typology of reasons for nonreporting proposed by Weiss (2011), who theorized that survivors' nonreporting decisions were based on denying criminal intent, denying serious injury, denying victim innocence, and rejecting a victim identity.In-depth qualitative interviews and focus groups have explored survivors' perspectives in even greater depth. From interviews with 29 sexual assault survivors, Patterson et al. (2009) found that survivors frequently worried that police would not or could not help them, and the decision to not report was often made based on a desire to protect themselves from the pain that engaging with police was expected to cause. Zweig and colleagues' (2014) focus groups similarly identified a theme of survivors not wanting to put themselves through the criminal legal process, as well as concerns related to shame, self-blame, fear of retaliation, and loss of privacy.Until the mid-2000s, survivors who did not report were often unable to access post-assault medical-forensic care (Lonsway & Archambault, 2011;Zweig et al., 2014). In many jurisdictions, police were responsible for authorizing SAEK collection, meaning that survivors who did not report or were deemed uncooperative were unable to access those services. This changed with the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) Reauthorization of 2005, which mandated that survivors have access to MFEs and SAEK collection regardless of whether they report the assault to police. The "alternative reporting options" now available to survivors vary by jurisdiction, but all require that survivors be able to access an MFE, have an SAEK collected, and have that SAEK stored for some period of time, during which the survivor can decide whether they want to report the assault (Lonsway et al., 2021). Because biological-forensic evidence can degrade within days, these alternative reporting options enable nonreporting survivors to capture timesensitive forensic evidence so that it is available should they later decide to report their assault.Research based on medical records indicates that 20% to 25% of sexual assault survivors who have an SAEK collected choose not to report their assault to police at that time (Campbell et al., 2021;Jones et al., 2009;Ledray, 2001), but relatively little is known about this population of survivors and their specific reasons for not reporting their assaults. Similar to what has been found in the larger reporting literature, the small body of research that has compared survivors who do not report their assault before or during SAEK collection to those who do has found that "stereotypical rape" characteristics often differentiate the two groups. Specifically, survivors who have an SAEK collected without reporting are more likely to have been intoxicated during the assault (Downing et al., 2022), and report that they knew the assailant (Schei et al., 2003;Stokbaek et al., 2021) and are less likely to have experienced an assault that involved penetration (Downing et al., 2022), physical force (Schei et al., 2003), or physical injury (Downing et al., 2022, Schei et al., 2003). Jones et al. (2009) queried these two groups of survivors directly by asking patients receiving medical-forensic care to complete a questionnaire after the exam had concluded. The questionnaire included a list of hesitations survivors may have about reporting the assault to police and respondents were asked to endorse any hesitations they had about reporting. Three differences emerged, with survivors who did not report before or during SAEK collection being significantly more likely to say they hesitated to report because they "knew the assailant" (54% vs. 23%), did "not want the assailant to go to jail" (66% vs. 9%), or were concerned that "police would be insensitive or blame" them for the assault (51% vs. 15%).Largely missing from the literature are reasons for not reporting described by this group of survivors in their own words. Sexual assault survivors who have medical forensic evidence collected but choose not to release the evidence to police for investigation at that time are a sizable subgroup with potentially unique needs, and understanding their reasons for not reporting could inform what services are offered to survivors in the aftermath of sexual assault. Therefore, the purpose of the current study was to explore the reasons for nonreporting given directly by survivors who had an SAEK collected but declined to report the assault to police at that time.

funding_statement: ConclusionsThe association between the inhibition component of EF, WM, and intelligence, and the lack of associations with shifting or PES in EF suggest that EF, WM, and intelligence might be linked through inhibition rather than monitoring and cognitive control, at least at kindergarten ages. Monitoring and cognitive control continue to develop further throughout childhood, and it may explain some of the shared variances between these three constructs only once it has reached a substantial level of variance and optimization and manifested in measures such as PES or the shift cost. A promising future direction is to longitudinally assess WM and intelligence in children and capture the age at which significant associations with indications of their cognitive control such as post-error slowing in EF may emerge. One practical implication of the current findings is that it may be promising to target training inhibition as a potential shared component between EF, WM, and intelligence to have an influence on all three constructs. This may be particularly important to reduce costs and maximize benefits when faced with intervention-related limitations. [101002163 || Migrants' Integration Policies Within Families and Across Generational GroupsThe second goal of the present study was to examine similarities and differences across the generations of adolescents, parents, and teachers. Are young people more inclusive than their elders? Overall, this study provided a nuanced pattern of differences. First, adolescents reported more positive attitudes toward the integration policies than their parents. The dyadic analyses also confirmed these results, according to which adolescents reported more positive attitudes toward integration policies compared to their mothers and fathers. While these findings point out differences within-family members, in line with generational theories' assumptions (Howe & Strauss, 2000;Strauss & Howe, 1991), it should be noted that they were characterized by small-tomoderate effect sizes, thus highlighting that intergenerational transmission processes are still operating (for reviews, see Degner & Dalege, 2013;Zagrean et al., 2022). Second, differences emerge also in the adolescents-teacher comparison but in the opposite direction, with the latter found to overcome the former in their attitudes toward integration policies and to be the most inclusive group of participants in the current study. Taken together, these findings underline that comparing adolescents with the older generations is not clear-cut but depends on the target group. Notably, adolescents develop their social attitudes in interaction with the different models provided by their main socialization contexts (i.e., family and school). funding_statement: FundingThe author(s) disclosed receipt of the following financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article: This work was supported by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (grant no. 435-2015-1825)  to the second author. || Grant: 435-2015-1825 || Judgment About Migrants' Language AbilityLanguage skills are widely considered to be among the most important competencies that migrants need to integrate into a new society (Lou, 2021;Pew Research Center, 2017). Despite the importance of communicative competence in the local language(s) for economic, civic and social engagement, migrants often have little opportunity or experience long delays in registering for language courses (Cowie & Delaney, 2019; Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages, 2013). The decline in migrants' language education opportunities has raised concerns about migrants' social equity (McHugh & Challinor, 2011;Simpson et al., 2007). In addition, language-related prejudice is manifested in interethnic interactions, such as when mainstream people avoid interaction with non-native speakers of the societal languages (Lippi-Green, 2012). These societal-level attitudes, policies, and prejudice can affect migrants' on-going acculturation experiences, language development, and psychological and physical well-being (Birney et al., 2020;Collins & Clément, 2012).Many social factors and psychological processes (e.g., political orientations, group identity, language-learning experiences, etc.) explain people's prejudice and discrimination against ethnolinguistic outgroups, including migrants, and one important aspect that social psychologists have focused on is people's perceptions of non-native speakers and their speech (Gluszek & Dovidio, 2010;Hansen & Dovidio, 2016;Kinzler et al., 2007). People who perceive migrants to have low fluency, strong accents, and low comprehensibility tend to have more negative attitudes toward migrants, and believe migrants are low in social status, less intelligent, credible, attractive, and hirable (Derwing et al., 2002;Dragojevic & Giles, 2016;Elliott & Leach, 2016;Fuertes et al., 2012;Hansen & Dovidio, 2016;Hosoda & Stone-Romero, 2010;Montgomery & Zhang, 2018). In addition, this research has shown that people who perceived migrants to have the potential to improve their language skills were also more supportive to migrants' language education and more willing to interact with them, even controlling for their perceptions about their language fluency.People's social inferences about whether migrants have the potential to improve their language skills are influenced by their fundamental beliefs about whether language learning ability is immutable (i.e., fixed mindsets) or malleable (i.e., growth mindsets; Lou & Noels, 2020a). Specifically, people who have a relatively fixed (vs. growth) language mindset tend to hold the view that people cannot change their ability to learn new languages. In contrast, people with a growth (vs. fixed) language mindset are more likely to believe they have control over their ability, attribute endorsed language challenges to controllable factors (e.g., effort, learning strategies; Hong et al., 1999), and thus believe that others also have more potential to learn and improve (Lou & Noels, 2020a). These findings are in line with the work on essentialism, which shows that the belief that a social group (e.g., gender, race, ethnolinguistic) has a fixed, inherent essence is associated with stereotypes and prejudice toward that group (Burgers & Beukeboom, 2020;Haslam et al., 2006). Indeed, research shows that fixed mindsets messages can increase essentialist beliefs about stigmatized groups (Levy et al., 2006).

coi_statement: Declaration of Conflicting InterestsThe author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interests with respect to the authorship and/or publication of this article. || Disclosure Patterns Among IPP-Included Suicide VictimsLastly, our findings show that more than one-third of suicide victims dealing with IPP had previous suicidal thoughts, as well as a history of attempted suicide. Additionally, about one-third of IPP-included suicide victims shared their suicidal ideation with others before committing suicide. This number indicates that suicide prevention opportunities exist. Notably, women struggling with IPP mostly tend to share their suicidal ideations with their partners. While this study was not designed to determine how intimate partners responded to such disclosures among these suicide victims, studies have found that invalidating responses toward suicide disclosure, including dismissing the suicidal partner's emotional experiences, downplaying the severity of their suicidality, or devaluing of the suicidal partner or the relationship, lead to worse outcomes (Love et al., 2021). These types of partner responses have the potential to intensify suicidal partners' feelings of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness (Van Orden et al., 2010), increasing the risk of suicide. Taken together, the previous and current findings demonstrate the importance of studying how intimate partners respond to disclosures and how those responses are perceived by individuals struggling with IPP and suicidality.Additionally, we identified that only 0.6% of IPP-included suicide victims disclosed their suicidal thoughts to healthcare professionals. Considering that about 40% of IPP-included suicide victims were receiving generalized mental health treatment and/or related counseling (e.g., had a medication prescription or met with a mental health professional and/or religious counselor within the 2 months prior to their death), there might be a possibility for service providers to miss identifying suicidal risk. This finding indicates that more research is needed to explore suicidal women's barriers to disclosing suicidal intentions to service providers like mental health professionals, marriage counselors, domestic violence advocates, or religious leaders who may be particularly well-placed to offer them support and help prevent their suicide. Notably, it is necessary to better understand the differences in disclosure and disclosure barriers to different types of mental health professionals and understand the variations in these service providers' responses.

funding_statement: Conclusion and Practical ImplicationsWe outlined and empirically demonstrated a cognitive spillover-crossover mechanism linking negative and positive rumination about work to the workers' and their partners' lower relationship satisfaction on the same day via workers' lower attention to the partner. Thereby, we showed that not only negative thoughts about work occupy their scarce attentional resources during their private time with the partner, but positive thoughts do this as well and thus can be as detrimental for a couple's daily relationship satisfaction as negative ones. However, we show that a couple is not helplessly at the mercy of work spilling over into and affecting their relationship quality. Sharing their thoughts about work with each other seems to be a practical way for couples to deal with the detrimental consequences of their ruminative thoughts about work on the quality of their relationship on that day. It is a way for couples to actively intervene in the chain of action and to take control of their own happiness. Furthermore, partners who talk about the work issues they ruminate about seem to even benefit from work rumination because this dyadic coping process increases partners' attention for each other and, in turn, also their relationship satisfaction. Talking about work, however, probably serves more than just dyadic support or elaboration and thus the release of attentional resources. Especially if romantic partners do not have similar occupations or work for the same organization, talking about work could be a chance to get a glimpse into each other's work lives which increases their intimacy.Funding Open access funding provided by University of Vienna. coi_statement: Declaration of Conflicting InterestsThe authors declared no potential conflicts of interests with respect to the authorship and/or publication of this article. || Benefits of DisclosureWhile little research has examined disclosure of violence specifically, numerous studies have highlighted the benefits of adolescents' general disclosure, defined as sharing information about oneself and one's experiences with others (Chen & Li, 2017;Elsharnouby & Dost-Gözkan, 2020;Mobasser et al., 2019). For example, adolescents with higher rates of general disclosure to parents and peers experience better mental well-being, life satisfaction, problem-solving confidence, and lower anxiety levels (Chen & Li, 2017;Elsharnouby & Dost-Gözkan, 2020). Additionally, lower levels of general disclosure to family or friends have been linked with higher risk of suicidal ideation and suicide attempts in adolescents (Horesh et al., 2004). Thus, general disclosure appears to play a protective role in adolescents' mental health.In addition to general disclosure, sharing experiences of stressful events with a confidant appears critical in helping adolescents, college students, and adults process and cope with these stressful events (Lepore et al., 2004;Slavin-Spenny et al., 2011;Ward et al., 2007). For example, greater disclosure of exposure to community violence has been linked to reduced substance abuse 1 year later in predominantly African American adolescents (Kliewer et al., 2017). Additionally, adolescents who witnessed intimate partner violence and disclosed this experience to a therapist showed fewer internalizing problems and decreased acceptance of violence (Graham-Bermann et al., 2011). Although little studied, disclosing violence exposure that occurred in other contexts such as in the peer environment or in a dating relationship may have similar benefits to those found for disclosing exposure to community violence or home violence victimization. Furthermore, it is important to understand with whom adolescents choose to share these experiences. When disclosing information about exposure to violence, youth may be seeking social support from others, which is an adaptive coping mechanism that facilitates the psychological processing of violence exposure (Graham-Bermann et al., 2011;Ozer & Weinstein, 2004;Paxton et al., 2004). The types of people with whom adolescents choose to share experiences of violence may also differ across contexts and types of violence, as well as across development throughout adolescence. || Patterns of Violence Exposure DisclosureOne of the few studies that examined adolescents' disclosure of victimization found that in a representative sample of Finnish 6th and 9th graders, 74% of those who experienced child abuse disclosed these experiences to someone. Specifically, 36% disclosed to their mother, 21% to their father, 14% to a sibling, 33% to a friend, 5% to a teacher, and 3% to a counselor (Lahtinen et al., 2022). However, only 4% of the sample reported child abuse, so it is unclear if similar rates and patterns of disclosure would be observed for other types of violence and populations with higher prevalence of violence exposure.Generally higher rates of disclosure were reported by ethnically diverse urban 7th graders from the United States (Ozer & Weinstein, 2004). Of the 76% that were exposed to community violence, 79% reported disclosing these experiences to their mother, 50% to their father, 55% to a sibling, 75% to a friend, 18% to a teacher, and 3% to a counselor. The differences in disclosure rates between child abuse in the Finnish study and community violence exposure in the U.S. study suggest that it may be easier for adolescents to disclose exposure to community violence than disclosing child abuse, perhaps because most child abuse is committed by the child's parents, which makes disclosing the experience more difficult (U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, 2022). However, cultural differences in disclosure may also explain some of the differences. Additionally, these differences may be due to different rates of disclosure for witnessing versus victimization by violence, which were combined into a single measure in the U.S. study. Very little is known on how disclosure rates may differ for violence exposure in different contexts, such as in the home environment, peer environment, the community, or in a dating context. It is possible that adolescents experience more shame or embarrassment about violence exposure occurring in family or dating environments as compared to violence exposure in a peer or community context, which may lead to less disclosure. Understanding if adolescents are less likely to disclose violence exposure in certain contexts may directly inform interventions that aim to increase disclosure of violence as a healthy coping mechanism among adolescents.Adolescents' disclosure of violent experiences may also change over the course of development. Longitudinal research suggests that general disclosure to parents decreases from age 12 to age 18 (Padilla-Walker et al., 2018), with disclosure shifting from parents to romantic partners and peers (Valkenburg et al., 2011). Thus, disclosure of exposure to violence may follow similar trends throughout adolescence. Indeed, in the aforementioned Finnish study of child abuse disclosure, the rates of disclosure to parents were lower in 9th compared to 6th graders (32% vs. 53% for mothers, 19% vs. 38% for fathers), whereas disclosure to friends was more common (36% vs. 22%) (Lahtinen et al., 2022). These cross-sectional results support the hypothesis that disclosure of violent experiences shifts from parents to friends across adolescence, but studies examining these trends longitudinally and across different types of violence exposure have not been conducted.Finally, disclosure rates of exposure to violence and targets of disclosure in African American samples have received little attention in the empirical literature. Since African American youth experience higher rates of violence than any other racial/ethnic group in the United States (Sickmund & Puzzanchera, 2014;Zimmerman & Messner, 2013), African American youth may perceive violence exposure as less unusual, which may in turn affect their disclosure behavior. Therefore, it is critical to understand patterns of disclosure of violence exposure in African American youth. || Sex Differences in Violence Exposure and DisclosureIn a national representative sample of children and adolescents, males report higher rates of victimization than females but did not differ in witnessing assault in the family or in the community (Finkelhor et al., 2015). In a sample of urban adolescents, males report higher rates of witnessing violence and victimization in the community than females (McDonald et al., 2011;Ruchkin et al., 2007). By contrast, sex differences in peer victimization have been less consistent across studies, with some research suggesting no sex differences (Felix & McMahon, 2007), but other research showing higher rates of physical peer victimization in males (Rueger & Jenkins, 2014). Furthermore, a few studies point to potential sex differences in dating violence exposure rates. For example, urban early adolescent males experience more physical dating violence than females (Lormand et al., 2013), but in urban middle and late adolescents, the prevalence of dating violence victimization appears similar across the sexes (Olshen et al., 2007).Additionally, females engage in higher rates of general disclosure than males (Soenens et al., 2006;Valkenburg et al., 2011). Although sex differences in disclosure of violence exposure specifically have been little investigated, adolescent males may show lower disclosure of these experiences because of societal pressure to conform to masculine stereotypes such as "emotional stoicism" and the need to project invulnerability (Oransky & Marecek, 2009). On the other hand, females are often encouraged to engage in relationships that involve high levels of self-disclosure (Underwood & Rosen, 2009). However, empirical research is needed to examine sex differences in disclosure of adolescents' experiences with different types of violence. || Differences in Disclosure Rates Across Confidants.To test the second hypothesis stating that youth are more likely to disclose violence exposure to parents and friends as compared to teachers, counselors, siblings and other relatives, significance tests for a difference in two proportions were conducted to pairwise compare rates of disclosure to parents and peers to rates of disclosure to teachers, counselors, siblings, and relatives at each time point. At T1, adolescents who disclosed any experiences of witnessing violence were more likely to disclose these experiences to parents as compared to teachers  (62% vs. 21%, z = 3.17, p < .001) and counselors (62% vs. 17%, z = 3.50, p < .001) and more likely to disclose these experiences to friends as compared to teachers (62% vs. 21%, z = 3.17, p < .001) and counselors (62% vs. 17%, z = 3.50, p < .001). The results showed no differences in the rates of disclosure of witnessing violence to parents, peers, siblings, and other relatives at T1. The results showed the same pattern at T2 with adolescents being more likely to disclose events of witnessing violence to parents as compared to teachers (59% vs. 16%, z = 3.55, p < .001) and counselors (59% vs. 16%, z = 3.55, p < .001) and adolescents being more likely to disclose witnessing violence to friends as compared to teachers (56% vs. 16%, z = 3.33, p < .001) and counselors (56% vs. 16%, z = 3.33, p < .001). The results showed no differences in the rates of disclosure for witnessing violence to parents, peers, siblings, and other relatives at T2. The same pattern was obtained at T3 with adolescents being more likely to disclose experiences of witnessing violence to parents as compared to teachers (66% vs. 31%, z = 2.80, p = .005) and counselors (66% vs. 22%, z = 3.55, p < .001) and more likely to disclose witnessing violence to friends as compared to teachers (66% vs. 31%, z = 2.80, p = .005) and counselors (66% vs. 22%, z = 3.55, p < .001). As in the previous time points, there were no differences in the rates of disclosure of witnessing violence to parents, peers, siblings, and other relatives at T3. In contrast to the results on witnessing violence, the results showed no differences in disclosure rates of victimization to parents as compared to teachers, counselors, siblings, or relatives at T1. However, adolescents were more likely to disclose victimization experiences to friends as compared to teachers at T1 (67% vs. 27%, z = 2.20, p = .028). Disclosure of violence victimization to friends did not differ from disclosure to counselors, siblings, or relatives at T1. At T2, adolescents who disclosed any violence victimization were more likely to disclose these experiences to parents as compared disclosing to teachers (61% vs. 11%, z = 3.12, p = .002) and counselors (61% vs. 6%, z = 3.50, p < .001). Adolescents were also more likely to disclose these experiences to friends as compared to teachers (83% vs. 11%, z = 4.33, p < .001), counselors (83% vs. 6%, z = 4.65, p < .001), siblings (83% vs. 39%, z = 2.71, p = .007), and non-parental relatives (83% vs. 33%, z = 3.04, p = .002). Disclosure rates for victimization to parents did not differ from disclosure rates to peers, siblings, or other relatives at T2. At T3, adolescents who disclosed any violence victimization were more likely to disclose these experiences to parents as compared to teachers (67% vs. 0%, z = 5.22, p < .001), counselors (67% vs. 11%, z = 4.22, p < .001), siblings (67% vs. 26%, z = 3.02, p = .003), and other relatives (67% vs. 26%, z = 3.02, p = .003). Similarly, adolescents were more likely to disclose these experiences to friends as compared to teachers (74% vs. 0%, z = 5.63, p < .001), counselors (74% vs. 11%, z = 4.68, p < .001), siblings (74% vs. 26%, z = 3.53, p < .001), and non-parental relatives (74% vs. 26%, z = 3.53, p < .001). Disclosure of victimization to parents did not differ from disclosure to friends at T3.Disclosure to Parents and Peers Over Time. To examine the third hypothesis stating that disclosure to parents decreases and disclosure to peers increases over time, significance tests for a difference in two proportions were conducted comparing rates of disclosure to parents and peers across the three time points for both witnessing violence and violence victimization. The results showed no differences in rates of disclosure to parents over time for both witnessing violence and victimization. Similarly, the results showed no differences in rates of disclosure to friends over time for both witnessing violence and victimization. However, the overall disclosure rate for victimization across confidants was higher at T3 as compared to T1 (52% vs. 29%, z = 2.42, p = .015). To confirm that this increase in disclosure was not due to participants not disclosing violence victimization being less likely to be retained at T3, a follow-up chi-square test examined whether adolescents who disclosed victimization at T1 were more or less likely to be retained than adolescents who did not disclose violence at T1. The results showed no significant differences between retained and not retained participants in disclosure of victimization at T1 (χ 2(1) = 0.47, p = .492).Sex Differences in Violence Exposure and Disclosure. To test the fourth hypothesis stating that females would have higher disclosure rates than males, chisquare difference tests were conducted for overall disclosure of witnessing violence and victimization at each time point. The results regarding sex differences in rates of exposure and disclosure of violence are reported for witnessing violence in Table 3 and victimization in Table 4. The results showed that males reported higher rates of dating violence victimization than females at T1 (68% vs. 39%, χ 2 (1) = 6.59, p = .010). Rates of exposure to witnessing violence or victimization did not differ by sex in any other context or time points. However, the results showed some sex differences in disclosure of violence exposure. Specifically, females were more likely to disclose events of dating violence victimization at T2 (39% vs. 8%, χ 2(1) = 6.21, p = .013). Moreover, females were more likely to disclose witnessing violence in any context at T3 (67% vs. 40%, χ 2(1) = 4.29, p = .038).    Statistics in bold are significant at p < 0.05. || Rates of Exposure and DisclosureThis study examined the rates of exposure and disclosure of experiences of violence across different contexts in a community sample of urban, lowincome African American youth followed from early to late adolescence. The findings showed high rates of violence exposure, especially in the form of witnessing conflict in the home environment, witnessing peer and community violence, and experiencing victimization in dating relationships.Although the majority of youth reported exposure to violence in the form of either witnessing or victimization, overall disclosure rates were low, with only 40%-53% of youth disclosing experiences of witnessing violence and 29%-52% disclosing experiences of violent victimization throughout adolescence. These disclosure rates are lower than in previous studies with ethnically diverse adolescents (Ozer & Weinstein, 2004). One explanation for low disclosure of exposure to violence in African American youth may be fear of losing autonomy through parental interference (Dinizulu et al., 2014). Previous research has shown that parents of African American adolescents who perceive the neighborhood environment as unsafe engage in heavier child monitoring, which adolescents may try to avoid through less disclosure (Jones et al., 2005). || Rates of Disclosure Across Contexts of Violence ExposureContrary to the hypothesis, the present findings suggest that adolescents' likelihood of disclosing experiences of witnessing violence to a confidant did not differ across the contexts in which the violence occurred. However, the findings partially support the hypothesis by suggesting that adolescents' likelihood of disclosing experiences of victimization differs across contexts, with adolescents being less likely to disclose experiences of dating violence victimization during both early and middle adolescence. It is possible that youth are most reluctant to disclose experiences of dating victimization to confidants due to feelings of shame or embarrassment or because they perceive others as unable to provide any assistance due to the private and intimate nature of a dating relationship (Fry et al., 2014;Rueda et al., 2015). Another reason for lower disclosure rates of dating violence victimization may be fear of losing autonomy. Previous studies showed that adolescents mentioned fear of having their activities restricted by adults as one barrier preventing them from disclosing dating violence victimization (Mapes & Cavell, 2021). Additionally, youth may be afraid that they would be told to end the romantic relationship and that their wishes would not be respected (Madkour et al., 2019;Ocampo et al., 2007;Rueda et al., 2015). Despite some evidence suggesting that adolescents experience similar barriers for disclosing violence in the peer environment, specifically fear of losing autonomy and social relationships (Dinizulu et al., 2014), no differences were found in disclosing violence victimization or witnessing violence in the peer environment compared to the home environment or community violence. || Differences in Disclosure Rates Across ConfidantsIn line with the hypothesis, the general pattern of the present results suggests that adolescents are most likely to disclose violence exposure including both witnessing violence and victimization to parents and peers and least likely to disclose these experiences to teachers and counselors. These results are consistent with findings of a recent study with Finnish adolescents, in which youth were also more likely to disclose experiences of violence exposure to parents and friends as compared to teachers, counselors, or siblings (Lahtinen et al., 2022). Similar results have been reported in an earlier study with U.S. early adolescents who were most likely to disclose experiences of violence to mothers and friends and least likely to disclose to teachers and counselors (Ozer & Weinstein, 2004). The present findings of friends being frequent sources for disclosure for African American youth are in line with a previous study involving White youth, which identified friends as primary recipients for disclosure of dating violence victimization during adolescents (Mapes & Cavell, 2021). The present findings suggest that adolescents are more likely to disclose experiences of violence to people with whom they share a personal relationship, such as parents and friends. Thus, these relationships may serve as safe spaces to discuss difficult personal experiences and as important sources of social support for dealing with traumatic experiences. The low rates of disclosure to teachers and counselors may reflect less close relationships adolescents have with their teachers, as well as the scarcity of counselors in under-resourced urban schools (Mann et al., 2019). The American School Counselors Association suggests a studentto-counselor ratio of 250 to 1; however, the National Average is 415 to 1 (ASCA, 2012), which does not allow the development of close studentcounselor relationships. Furthermore, school counselors are often burdened with additional tasks that reduce their ability to meet with and support students (Lewis et al., 2022). || Disclosure to Parents and Peers Over TimeContrary to the hypothesis, there was no decrease in the disclosure rates of any violence exposure to parents and no increase in the disclosure rates of any violence exposure to peers over time. This finding contradicts the literature that suggests general disclosure shifts from parents to friends as adolescents mature (Padilla-Walker et al., 2018;Valkenburg et al., 2011). However, given the present study's focus on disclosure of exposure to violence specifically, these findings may indicate that disclosure about exposure to violence is not a disclosure topic that shifts from parents to peers with increasing age during adolescence. Indeed, some research suggests that adolescents value both disclosure to friends and parents from early adolescence to late adolescence (Mobasser et al., 2019). Future research should recruit a larger sample to replicate the present results and to untangle the difference between general disclosure and disclosure about exposure to violence throughout adolescence.Interestingly, disclosure to any confidant for overall victimization was higher at age 18 when compared to age 13. These findings may reflect the increase in autonomy with age. Parents of African American adolescents who perceive the neighborhood environment as unsafe engage in heavier child monitoring, which early adolescents may try to avoid through less disclosure (Jones et al., 2005). As adolescents enter late adolescence, they may be less concerned with their parents restricting their movement and become more willing to discuss their experiences. A similar process may unfold toward other potential confidants as adolescents mature and become less prone to spotlight effects (Rankin, 2004), allowing them to feel more comfortable disclosing experiences of victimization. || Sex Differences in Violence Exposure and DisclosureThe present results suggest that males experience higher rates of dating victimization at age 13, which is consistent with some previous research (Lormand et al., 2013). Given the more mature pubertal development of adolescent girls compared to boys during early adolescence (Slyper, 2006), males may not yet have a physical advantage and girls are exposed to higher levels of stress during puberty (Natsuaki et al., 2009), which may make females more likely to act aggressively toward their dating partners during early adolescence. This interpretation is further supported by the present results showing no sex differences in dating violence victimization at age 16 and 18, which is consistent with previous findings (Olshen et al., 2007).Interestingly, females were more likely to disclose dating violence victimization at age 16 as well as 18 compared to males. An explanations for this sex difference may be the conformity to gender stereotypes by males such as being "tough" and not being "emotional" (Cunningham & Meunier, 2004;Cunningham et al., 2013). These attitudes typically emphasize non-disclosure of emotions and personal issues to others, as emotional stoicism is seen as one way to project imperviousness (Scharrer, 2001;Wade & Rochlen, 2013). Disclosing dating violence victimization involves admitting that they had been victimized by a dating partner, and males may therefore refrain from disclosing dating violence victimization. Another explanation for this difference may be the different ways in which males and females are socialized. Females are typically encouraged to develop relationships that involve high levels of self-disclosure (Underwood & Rosen, 2009). As youth enter late adolescence, females may have better support networks to whom they feel more comfortable disclosing exposure to violence, whereas for males self-disclosure is not a common behavior that is further reduced by having less close relationships with others.

What happens in an abusive relationship is often messy and complicated, and such relationships typically intensify power dynamics (Lundgren, 2004). Indeed, to the extent that variance in certain contextual conditions may weaken attitude-behavior correspondence, it is not surprising that Smit and Montag- Smit (2019) found the correspondence between trait pay information search preferences and past pay information-seeking behavior to be contingent on employer pay communication policy.If, as suggested by Smit and Montag-Smit (2019), employer pay communication policy serves as a contextual factor moderating the link between employee pay information search preferences and actual seeking behavior, it is conceivable that employer pay communication policy also moderates the link between an individual's willingness to exchange their own pay information and the likelihood that they will disclose their pay. What is uncertain, however, is the form that this conditioning effect will take. We posit that unless employees engage in deliberative thinking about the potential implications of pay information sharing in more (versus less) restrictive pay communication contexts, the effect of pay communication context is likely to be automatic, driven by heuristic processes amplifying the association between the individual's willingness to disclose their pay and the probability of their actual disclosure. || | Pay disclosureAt T2 we asked participants to disclose their actual pay bonus in the previous tax year ( pay disclosure). Participants were asked to "select from the drop-down menu to specify the exact amount of any 'annual bonus' (i.e., total of individual and team bonuses) received in the most recent tax year in thousands/hundreds of dollars". Those who provided their exact bonus pay information were coded 1 and those who selected "prefer not to disclose" were coded 0. || | Actual pay disclosureA series of logistic regression models were estimated to test predictors of actual pay disclosure. The main effects reported in Model 1 of Table 3 reveal that females were significantly less likely to report actual pay (estimate = À0.59, p < .05), that willingness to disclose was a strong positive predictor of actual disclosure (estimate = 0.77, p < .001), and that employer pay communication restrictiveness was positively related to actual disclosure (estimate = 0.33, p < .01).Hypothesis 3a proposed a two-way interaction between willingness to disclose and the restrictiveness of employer pay communication policy. The results in Model 2 of Table 3 provide no support for this hypothesis (estimate = À.05, ns). It is likely, however, that this non-significant finding reflects the differential impact of the random assignment to deliberate thinking proposed as the higher-order threeway interaction in Hypothesis 3b. Model 3 of Table 3 provides the results of the three-way interaction (estimate = À0.24, p < .10).Hypothesis 3b was supported with the proposed 3-way interaction significant at a 90% confidence level. The form of the interaction (plus or minus one standard deviation for employer pay restrictiveness) is presented in Figure 4 and reflects the inherent non-linear nature of logistic regression (Long & Freese, 2014). Results are consistent with the hypothesized form, suggesting a less than a 5% chance of obtaining the observed form of the relationship if the null hypothesis was true (i.e., a p-value of less than .05 using a one-tailed test). funding_statement: Suicidal risks among post-incarcerated adultsThis study drew on the insights from two theoretical perspectives of suicide that have been developed based on studies of the general population: hopelessness theory of suicide (Abramson et al., 1989;Kleiman et al., 2014) and interpersonal theory of suicide (Christensen et al., 2013;Van Orden et al., 2010). Hopelessness theory of suicide is a diathesis-stress theory, which maintains that when individuals who have a negative cognitive style experience negative events, they would expect a negative future-a feeling of hopelessness. A high level of hopelessness contributes to the risk of suicide (Abramson et al., 1989). The second theoretical perspective-interpersonal theory of suicide-conceptualizes "thwarted belongingness" as a significant marker of suicide behavior (Van Orden et al., 2010). Thwarted belongingness is a feeling of isolation, which results from an unmet need for belongingness (Joiner, 2005). People who become suicidal often have feelings of isolation and alienation (Christensen et al., 2013).Although these two theories are derived from studies on the general population, a study on post-incarcerated individuals can benefit from drawing on some insights from these perspectives. The transition from prison to community is a challenging process that is characterized by life events closely related to hopelessness and social isolation. First, post-incarcerated individuals may experience alienation and rejection from family and community. Many individuals face severe difficulty in reestablishing broken family ties when reentering the community (e.g., Liu & Visher, 2019;Mowen et al., 2019). By using qualitative interviews, Breese and colleagues (2000) found that some respondents were treated like the "black sheep" of the family (p. 14) when they came home, and that some respondents' families had moved away from the area during their incarceration. Social isolation is also found to be triggered by the stigma of a criminal record (Harding et al., 2019). A study found that after release, respondents worried that it was difficult to be socially accepted again after imprisonment, to renew relationships with old friends, and to play an important role in other people's lives (Liu et al., 2021).Besides relational issues, financial hardship is another dimension of stressor that can potentially contribute to suicide. The majority of released prisoners report difficulties gaining employment during reentry, due to the fact that long prison sentences deprive them of the opportunity to gain work experience and that job networks are severed (Liu, 2022;Western, 2018). Most post-incarcerated individuals go back to neighborhoods with low average income, high poverty rate, and few job opportunities (Western & Sirois, 2019). Employers may worry that a person with a criminal record is less trustworthy and reliable and thus are less likely to employ them (Pager et al., 2009;Western & Sirois, 2019), which further decreases their chance of employment. Various accesses to financial support from family, friends, and government can alleviate the financial hardship of former prisoners; however, these sources of support are not always available (Arditti & Few, 2008;Mallik-Kane & Visher, 2008). People with criminal records are often denied access to public housing projects, and a disproportionate percentage of reentering persons experience homelessness or residential instability after release (Harding et al., 2019;Morenoff & Harding, 2014). Men with incarceration histories were twice as likely to experience housing instability, and four times more likely to experience homelessness than the general population (Greenberg & Rosenheck, 2008;Geller & Curtis, 2011). For example, in a large study of all New York State prison releases to New York City, Metraux and Culhane (2004) found that within two years 11.4% of the study group had entered a New York homeless shelter (2004, p. 139).

coi_statement: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Empirical research suggests that married women may more commonly experience spousal pornography use as a relational attachment threat and are more likely to experience negative relational outcomes such as distress and loss of trust. The purpose of this study was to develop a grounded theory of married women's response to the discovery or disclosure of spousal pornography use. This study included the experiences of 30 married women who reported spousal pornography use as a threat to relational attachment, who chose to remain with their spouse, and who reported evidence of individual and relational healing thereafter. The research question, “How do married women describe the experience of learning of their spouse's pornography use and the individual and relationship sequelae that follow?” was explored using grounded theory methods to analyze deidentified blogpost accounts emphasizing response to a spouse's pornography use. The results describe a process model highlighting three interrelated informant categories—emotional response, mental response, and physical response—and one resultant category—behavioral response. Implications include (a) the importance of open communication regarding pornography use within relationships, (b) the necessity for individual and relational healing following betrayal trauma, and (c) the role of therapeutic intervention in shaping adaptive healing processes.</jats:p> || Crawford M. funding_statement: Funding informationSociety for the Psychological Study of Social Issues, Grant/Award Number: Grant-in-Aid || Contact with immigrantsThe Developmental Intergroup Contact Survey (Crystal et al., 2008) was adapted to measure participants' contact with immigrants. Four items were used to measure the quantity of friendships and direct contact participants had with people from different countries (e.g., 'At school/outside of school/in your neighborhood how many friends do you have who are from a different country but now live in the USA?'). Responses were given using a 4-point Likert-type scale from 1 = none, to 4 = many. This scale had an overall Cronbach's α = .75, with slightly lower reliability for participants of nonimmigrant background (α = .71), compared to those of immigrant background (α = .77). In previous studies, this measure was correlated with cross-race friendship and attitudes toward outgroups (Ruck et al., 2011). || Differential pathways for immigrant victims of bullyingWhile the desire for social contact was relevant for the likelihood to intervene on behalf of both Arab and Latine victims of bullying, contact with immigrants was only important for Latine victims. This was demonstrated by an association involving shared immigrant background which indicated that immigrant-origin youth who shared ethnic identity with immigrant victims (92% of the immigrantorigin youth reported Latine heritage) also have more contact with peers from similar immigration backgrounds and this increased experience was associated with higher likelihood to help a Latine victim. It is unclear if shared ethnic identity was driving participants' responses or whether it was the opportunity for contact that was available. More research is needed to clarify this, perhaps by sampling adolescents of diverse immigrant backgrounds (such as Asian American youth) and asking them about intervening on behalf of Latine victim in regions where there are ample opportunities to engage with Latine peers. Additionally, even though participants were asked about contact with immigrant-origin peers it may be that participants were thinking about ethnic group membership as opposed to a broader immigrant social category when completing the contact measure, because they did complete these items after being introduced to the victim. Shared-immigrant background, however, was not important for intentions to intervene on behalf of an Arab immigrant peer. This is counter to research and theoretical approaches that emphasize the importance of superordinate identities, such as those based on immigrant background, which highlight similarities among individuals as opposed to more specific identities, such as ethnicity, which may draw attention to differences (Dovidio et al., 2017). One explanation for this lack of association for Arab victims of bullying could be that shared group membership works only when there are opportunities for contact and does not promote a desire or interest per se in interacting with immigrant-origin peers who are not around to interact with. However, when opportunities for direct contact are limited, as they were for this sample with peers of Arab backgrounds, a desire for social contact becomes more salient.These differing pathways may begin to explain why existing anti-bullying interventions are not as effective in heterogeneous schools. The multi-group analysis suggested that contact with immigrants may not generalize to increased intentions to intervene on behalf of victims from varying immigrant backgrounds (Latine and Arab). Thus, interventions may seek to draw from the research on extended or indirect contact (Aboud & Spears Brown, 2013;Cameron et al., 2011;Pettigrew et al., 2007), to encourage intervention on behalf of victims of bias-based bullying in contexts where there may not be ample opportunities for direct contact. Nevertheless, contact with immigrants was important for victims where opportunities for contact were available (i.e., Latine background). In fact, as expected, the model for the Latine victim resulted in more variance explained in bystander intentions to intervene in response to bias-based bullying (52.3%) compared to the model for the Arab victim (14.1%). || AC K NOW L E D G M E N T SThis study was supported by Society for the Psychological Study of Social Issues-2018 Grant-in-Aid.

funding_statement: ConclusionsDespite the above-mentioned limitations, this study represents an innovative approach for operationalizing RDoC based on recently developed psychoneurometric methods. Our main goal was not to present definitive findings but rather to pursue a new neurobehavioral approach in which individual differences recorded from a multi-level analysis can guide research toward new conceptions of the way we assess psychopathological phenomena (Yancey et al., 2016). Brain and physiological methods remain underdeveloped for accomplishing the ambition of defining new neurobehavioral assessment protocols with clinical utility (Patrick et al., 2019). Thus, there is a need for a systematic research strategy aimed at establishing multimethod clinical assessments to better understand mental health outcomes.The psychoneurometric approach can provide a compelling pathway for achieving this goal within the near term, even if several methodological challenges exist (e.g., normative-sample datasets including data from different domains of measurement). Our analyses revealed a sufficient degree of correlation between units of analysis to obtain common factors reflecting RDoC's domains of functioning. Furthermore, Performance Monitoring, Inhibitory Control, and Sustained Threat constructs were correlated with internalizing constituents, while externalizing was uniquely correlated with Sustained Threat. These findings underscore that variations in RDoC-related processes may play a pivotal role in multiple clinical problems and may reflect transdiagnostic, cross-cutting mechanisms that differently account for patterns of homotypic and heterotypic continuity among disorders described in the psychopathological spectrum.From this perspective, the RDoC matrix can be an interesting avenue to advance our knowledge of the existing models of psychopathology, such as HiTOP (Kotov et al., 2017). Ultimately, bridging RDoC and dimensional models of psychopathology may accelerate translational neuroscience.Funding Open access funding provided by FCT|FCCN (b-on). coi_statement: Disclosure statementThe authors declare that they have no conflict of interest. || Communal orientation and self-disclosureAccording to the TRRL, a communal orientation promotes relational investments (Afifi et al., 2016). The theory provides a broad interpretation of investment (or maintenance), describing it as "prosocial, daily verbal and nonverbal behaviors, perceptions, and actions that allow relational partners and family members to become resilient and thrive" (Afifi et al., 2016, p. 664). One important way individuals can invest in their relationship is by engaging in daily self-disclosure to their partner, which entails sharing their thoughts and feelings and maintaining an open line of communication. Self-disclosure has been defined as "an act of intimacy [that] serves as a maintenance strategy" (Sprecher & Hendrick, 2004, p. 857) and is similar to the concepts of both openness (a communicative relational maintenance strategy; Stafford & Canary, 1991) and relationship talk, two components of the integrative model of relationship maintenance believed to enhance relationships (Ogolsky et al., 2017). Prior work has revealed associations between both one's own (e.g., Afifi et al., 2019) and a partner's (e.g., McAninch et al., 2022) communal orientation and relational maintenance behaviors. As such, we predicted a positive association between one's own and their partner's communal orientation and daily self-disclosure: H3: Individuals' own (a; actor effect) and their partner's (b; partner effect) communal orientation will be positively associated with their own self-disclosure. H4: Individuals' own (a; actor effect) and their partner's (b; partner effect) communal orientation will be positively associated with their perceptions of their partner's selfdisclosure. || Communal orientation, self-disclosure, and thrivingCommunal orientation is thought to promote relational investments and maintenance behaviors, such as engaging in daily self-disclosure, leading to greater perceived emotional resources, less threatening stress appraisals, and individual and relational thriving (Afifi et al., 2016;Zamanzadeh & Afifi, 2019). Conversely, couples who have failed to invest in their relationship and do not enact relationship-maintaining behaviors (e.g., self-disclosure) appraise stressors as more threatening, which can harm the relationship by depleting emotional resources and contributing to relational load (i.e., relational strain due to chronic stress, conflict, and/or a lack of investment; Afifi et al., 2016Afifi et al., , 2019)). Afifi et al. (2016) assert that it is "primarily the everydayness of relationships," or daily investment, that makes relational partners feel supported and secure and ultimately contributes to resilience (p. 667). Marini and colleagues (2018) also point to the value of daily assessments of relational behaviors (such as self-disclosure) for understanding relational dynamics as they unfold in everyday life.Tests of the TRRL have demonstrated that increasing prosocial communication (e.g., affectionate or supportive communication) provides benefits for individuals and relationships (Afifi et al., 2019;2020a;2020b;Guntzviller & Wang, 2019). During difficult times, in particular, behaviors that reinforce an interest and investment in one's relationship can positively impact both individual and relational thriving. For example, parents who engaged in more positive communication and relational maintenance strategies regarding their child's type 1 diabetes reported less conflict and stress (Afifi et al., 2019). Other research employing the TRRL similarly revealed that warm and supportive maintenance behaviors foster resilience when navigating transitions, struggles, and discrepancies in one's identity (Rubinsky, 2019;Waldron & Farnworth, 2020). In the context of romantic partnerships, self-disclosure within couples has been associated with both individual (e.g., self-esteem, responsiveness) and relational (e.g., satisfaction, commitment) outcomes (Sprecher & Hendrick, 2004). Daily reports of one's own selfdisclosure and a partner's self-disclosure also predict greater intimacy both directly and indirectly (partial mediation) through perceived partner responsiveness (Laurenceau et al., 2005). In other words, day-to-day disclosures are linked to positive relational outcomes, and feeling supported and cared for partially explains that association.The TRRL also notes the power of communication to uplift one's partner (Afifi et al., 2016). In fact, individuals may be even more influenced by their partner's investment than their own (Zamanzadeh & Afifi, 2019). As such, individuals who perceive that both they and their partner are investing in the relationship (i.e., one's perception of their own selfdisclosure and one's perception of their partner's self-disclosure) may be more likely to report that they are thriving and their relationship is thriving in the face of the COVID-19 pandemic. Indeed, positive communication has been associated with better relationship functioning during COVID-19 (e.g., Brisini et al., 2018;Knoster et al., 2020;Li & Samp, 2021). Prior work also indicates that relational investments mediate the association between communal orientation and relationship outcomes. For example, communal orientation has been indirectly associated with both one's own and their partner's relational load and resilience through maintenance behaviors (Afifi et al., 2021;McAnich et al., 2022).Taken together, we predicted that a mediation relationship would exist when examining patterns across the week (i.e., "accrued maintenance" in the parlance of the TRRL; Afifi et al., 2016), such that both one's own and their partner's communal orientation at baseline would be associated with one's own greater self-disclosure each day, as well as greater perceptions of partner self-disclosure each day, and that both one's own self-disclosure and their perceptions of their partner's self-disclosure would predict greater relational and individual thriving over the course of the week (see Figure 1 1 ). Such predictions align with both the original theorizing in the TRRL (Afifi et al., 2016), as well as with tests of the theory that have similarly positioned maintenance or investment as a mediator between communal orientation and resilience (e.g., Afifi et al., 2021;McAninch et al., 2022). Although we expected that communal orientation would directly associate with self-disclosure (H1/H2) and thriving (H3/H4), building upon prior TRRL scholarship, we also expected that self-disclosure would partially account for the association between communal orientation and thriving. In other words, one of the reasons that communal orientation leads to thriving is by promoting greater self-disclosure. Thus, the following hypotheses were advanced: H5: Individuals' own (a) and their perceptions of their partner's (b) self-disclosure will partially mediate the association between self-/partner-reported communal orientation and individual thriving. Similarly, partner-reported (c) and partner-reported perceived partner (d) self-disclosure will partially mediate the association between self-/partnerreported communal orientation and individual thriving. 2 H6: Individuals' own (a) and their perceptions of their partner's (b) perceptions of the other partner's self-disclosure will partially mediate the association between self-/partnerreported communal orientation and relational thriving. coi_statement: Conflicts of Interest:The authors declare no conflict of interest. || Self-Disclosure on Psychological Home in CyberspaceCompared to conventional face-to-face communication, online environments have been proven to feature a greater extent of self-disclosure. Moreover, users tend to disclose more information when anonymous [30,31]. This is because they feel safe when they do not see the people they are addressing and can focus on the phrasing of their words and the expression of their emotions. In the study of how Internet users establish interpersonal relationships, Parks and Floyd [32] discovered that people are more likely to speak honestly online than in the real world. This also confirmed the hypothesis of Rheingold [33]-people not only establish substantial relationships through computers, but also express their true feelings more easily because the anonymity of the Internet environment provides a sense of freedom and reduced restraint. Online self-disclosure has been widely discussed and applied by scholars in relation to e-commerce and Internet services [34,35]. Ledbetter [36] also proved that online self-disclosure and social connection are the primary motivators for the use of social media. Therefore, the main initial objective of social media was to establish interpersonal relationships on the Internet. Hagel and Armstrong [37] identified interpersonal relationships as a basic motivation of virtual communities. Among the motivations of Facebook users discussed by Alhabash et al. [38], interpersonal relationships were a key motivation. Self-disclosure is a factor in the establishment of interpersonal relationships because it increases intimacy [39,40].According to the aforementioned studies, interpersonal relationships are a core motivation for social media use, and self-disclosure is an essential step for people to develop interpersonal relationships in virtual communities. For instance, the wedge model of self-disclosure proposed by Altman and Taylor [41] indicated a causal relationship between self-disclosure and intimacy. Lin and Chu [42] found users of Facebook will have more degrees of self-disclosure when emotionally supported by friends, thereby intimacy emerged. However, it happened when young people posted photos about enjoying an expensive meal, and then was censured by their parents below these photos. Some adolescents expressed agreement with the lifestyle of goblin mode, but were soon criticized by their parents for laziness and passivity just below this comment. These interactions made young people feel embarrassed and could suppress the desire to self-disclose. Therefore, this study inferred that, in the case of parental involvement, users are unable to develop interpersonal relationships effectively because of their inability to disclose themselves, resulting in negative relationships (i.e., behaviors such as discontinuous use or social media platform switching).

coi_statement: <jats:sec id="S2056472423001412_sec_a1"><jats:title>Aims</jats:title><jats:p>Access to a healthy environment offers broad health benefits and has been declared a human right (UNHCR, 2021). However, despite the release of position statements by royal colleges on the climate and ecological emergency, there appears to have been limited opportunities for dissemination and sharing of knowledge, understanding and opportunities for action for many doctors and medical students in the North of Scotland. Hence, this project was aimed to create awareness on the importance of nature connectedness and explore its association with good physical and mental health and well-being. It was also so the medical students can understand the relationship between nature connectedness and the experiences in nature through active observation and hands-on engagement activities alongside acknowledging already active allies providing practical environmental volunteering activities.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec id="S2056472423001412_sec_a2"><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>9 Medical students, 3 Core Psychiatry Trainees, 1 Psychologist and 1 Child and Adolescent Psychiatrist met at Trees for Life, Dundreggan. We were introduced to 2.5 hours of mindful grounding techniques, mindful eating, connecting with nature through art along with sensory exercises such as tree hugging and trust building activities by Nature for Health. We interacted in group work to design nature-based activities that can be used in clinical practice to improve mental well-being in people living with OCD, depression, ADHD, trauma and eco-anxiety.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec id="S2056472423001412_sec_a3"><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>Learning experience amidst nature was well received by participants who also gained positive effects on their own personal well-being. The project successfully brought the participants together to access, care for and enjoy green spaces whilst learning about allied programs available in the community. The participants also learnt how nature can aid mental health recovery and well-being, whilst giving people a chance to do their bit towards the fight against climate change.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec id="S2056472423001412_sec_a4"><jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title><jats:p>We suggest to incorporate teachings on climate change in medical education with consideration on using green spaces as delivery sites to enhance nature connectedness (local green social prescribing opportunities such as Green Walking, Green Gym, conservation volunteering, city farms, forest schools by The Conservation Volunteers, The Wildlife Trusts and the ‘Rewild and Recover’ programme from Trees of Life). We also suggest to promote our future healthcare professionals to collaborate with other groups linking nature restoration to human health and well-being. Awareness on benefits of nature connectedness should become one of the most important aspects of medical education in this century to foster a generation of healthcare professionals with pro-nature attitudes and active engagements with the natural world.</jats:p></jats:sec>
