funding_statement: 'Reconstructing' the MIT Fund: 'sedimentations' as criteria, dis/ organising as a methodThe reconstruction of the MIT's archival collection, which at the moment constitutes the core of the MIT's historical archive, represented two things for our working group: on the one hand, we had to get to the heart of what it means to organise a trans archive, with its possibilities, complexities and critical issues; on the other hand, we had to trace our genealogies. In our work as archivists/activists, we have tried to question traditional archival epistemologies. Indeed, studying archival practices has meant that we have had to challenge our critical epistemologies, that is, the 'diverging' way in which we wished 'to know' and 'to let others know' what had emerged during the reconnaissance phase (Arondekar and et al, 2015;Bourcier, 2020;Marshall et al., 2015). We understand the archival series, the archival units and the documentary units as 'sedimented embodied histories' (Lau, 2018) of collective and subjective bodies, individual and associative experiences, histories that do not remain in their own separate place but intertwine with each other, continuously disorienting and re-orienting the identity of the MIT Fund. In our practices, we took inspiration from Porpora Marcasciano's activism and literary production by giving value to the meticulous process of collecting and preserving the trans past, weaving it together with the trans present. At the beginning of the 2000s, Marcasciano (2002) described her pioneering work of collecting trans life and trans activist histories in her book Tra le rose e le viole (Among Roses and Violets), a seminal history of trans experiences in Italy from the end of the 1950s to the present day, which the author reconstructs through stories and firsthand accounts -as throwing a net in the open sea to then hoist it back on board full of unknown and unexpected material. Almost 20 years later, in the MIT's storeroom, we opened drawers (occasionally also with Porpora), unpacked cardboard boxes and clipboards, and hoisted back more than 5000 documents of different kinds, mainly from the late 1970s up to the present, although some pieces dated back to the 1940s.At first, struck by the desire and the felt necessity to trace a hidden political history and to make it accessible, we were tempted to make sense of the content of the individual documents, to link them together to rebuild pieces related to this history, and to allow them to make sense for the people who would have access to them. We had to take a transversal step back, stumbling on our own convictions about what it means to 'order', 'preserve', 'describe' and 'enhance' in a critical way, overcoming our own prejudices about the practice of documentation 'ordering' from an archival perspective. To 'preserve' the documents of the MIT Fund in this process did not mean 'to store as it is', but to 'let ourselves be disoriented' by the original logics of conservation and to render those logics visible and traceable, even in their complexity and in their (apparent) disorder. Indeed, if every single document in the fund has a historical value and tells a story, the reasons for which certain documents -apparently very different, almost irreconcilable -end up in the same clipboard while others -typologically and thematically similar -do not, also have a historical explanation.In this regard, the handwritten letters and drawings by E. (a friend and regular visitor of the MIT association in the 1990s) not only speak of the author and her trans history, but are in dialogue with -among others -the political statements that the MIT signed regarding the rights of trans people in the workplace and the political campaigns for the fight against HIV/AIDS and more inclusive access to sexual health. The press review, whose content contained many reports of institutional violence against trans people and sex workers, engages in a dialogue -and is often preserved together -with flyers of political events and grassroots magazines that document the struggles promoted by the MIT, the Comitato per i diritti civili delle prostitute (Committee for the civil rights of prostitutes) and other collectives active at the time.These 'sedimentations' (or the occasional lack thereof) speak to us about the organisational histories, the personalities, the affective bonds, the conflicts, the phases and the situated political necessities of an association as dynamic and long-lived as the MIT. For instance, we noted how administrative documents have never been preserved in a systematic and thematic way; we found them together with the MIT's public statements related to the organisation of demonstrations, correspondence and press clippings, thereby demonstrating that the act of preservation was not an act for its own sake but had the political function of supporting actions to change the socio-cultural reality of the time.This choice could be linked to the willingness -formally demonstrated and carried out by the association (and the individuals who composed it) -to construct collective memory as a daily political practice (through the collection and conservation of documents of various kinds, although often not in a structured or systematised way), through which the members of the association gave meaning to events and experiences belonging to a specific social and political context (Halbwachs, 1992). This willingness went hand in hand with a desire to create visibility and change in the present through a constant presence in the public space, thanks to the development of projects and services dedicated to trans people.Reconstructing the MIT Fund therefore did not imply making every single document accessible, but describing the sedimentations that characterise the archival units to make the 'dis/organisation' (Brewis et al., 2014;Cooper, 1986;Virtú, 2020) of the nexuses between and among these units visible. Our descriptions indicate which archival units we assembled and titled, and which archival units we inherited as they were. As in a genealogy 'of choice', the original logic of conservation (which may have even been modified several times in the past) thus merges with our touch, and we avoid letting our work 'pass' (Stone, 1991) as a 'natural' systematisation of the parts or a 'neutral' ordering. 7  Moreover, every document type opens the doors to a different way of looking at the history of the MIT and at different, interdependent methodologies. A good example is the strong connection between photographic documents and oral testimonies. While identifying and describing the context of the photographic documents held at the MIT Fund, we have collectively employed individual memory as a tool for the inventory of the materials, which in many cases, concerned collective events and activities of the MIT association and LGBTQ+ movements in Italy. At the same time, photographs have offered precious support in the process of collecting oral history testimonies, as the people we interviewed opened their 'private photographic funds' to us while going through and evoking past events in their lives (Dragojlovic, 2018), in a continuous coming and going of memories between public and personal experiences (Image 3).

funding_statement: FundingThis work was supported by Forte: Swedish Research Council for Health, Working Life and Welfare (grant number 2021-00023), Swedish Research Institute in Istanbul, and the European Commission (Central Asian Law, grant number 870647 and MOCCA, grant number 101085855). || Grant: 2021-00023 || Grant: 870647 || Grant: 101085855 || Setting the Context: Uzbek Migrants in SwedenThe Uzbek community in Sweden is quite new and small. Yet, it is one of the fastest growing communities in the country and stands out in regard to the share of undocumented migrants in its ranks. Officially, there are more than 5,000 individuals originating from Uzbekistan living in Sweden (SCB, 2023), but the number of undocumented migrants from Uzbekistan in the country is believed to be between 15,000 and 20,000, or three to four times more than official figures, as confirmed by numerous informal community leaders among Uzbeks. The fact that the number of Uzbek applicants for asylum in Sweden and the share of rejected applications remain quite high (Migrationsverket, 2023) for a country where there is no ongoing conflict, and where the situation with human rights compliance has improved in recent years, indicates that a significant number of the applicants are, in reality, economic migrants seeking legal ways to reside in Sweden.Many Uzbek migrants in Stockholm live in shared rented apartments as their undocumented status may prevent them from renting accommodation independently. Sharing an apartment also allows them to save on living costs. I have seen cases when even documented migrants preferred this way to share expenses. Undocumented migrants also fear that seeking medical care or assistance from social welfare programs could jeopardise their presence in the country and lead to negative repercussions (Jönsson, 2014;Lundberg & Spång, 2017). Some employers, such as pizzerias or companies working with subcontracts in the construction or cleaning sectors may hire undocumented migrants due to their vulnerability and willingness to accept lower wages and subpar working conditions. As a result, in some cases Uzbek migrants may face exploitation, long working hours and limited job security. In some cases, employers may also provide housing to their undocumented employees, tying their living situation to their employment, further exacerbating their dependence and vulnerability.Uzbekistan, with a population of 36 million people, is the most densely populated country in Central Asia. Declining living conditions, high levels of unemployment, low salaries and poor human rights conditions in the country have led several million Uzbeks to seek better lives abroad. The majority of these migrants go to visa-free countries such as Russia, Turkey and Kazakhstan. However, the number of Uzbeks working in visa-imposed countries such as Japan, South Korea, the Gulf States, the Schengen zone and the U.S. has also significantly grown in recent years. Since salaries in these countries are much higher than in visa-free countries, many of them put in a lot of effort to obtain visas despite heavy bureaucratic obstacles and high fees charged by document facilitators.The Schengen zone, and the Nordic countries in particular, is one of the most desired destinations among Uzbek would-be migrants. However, due to the lack of Swedish or other Nordic country embassies in Uzbekistan, many Uzbeks attempt to reach these destinations through other Schengen countries that have their embassies in Tashkent. Obtaining work visas, or in some cases tourism or education visas, to Poland and the Baltic states is not impossible. There is a thriving business of document facilitators who help 'applicants' not only in obtaining visas, residence, work, driving and other permits, but also in matching with potential employers and landlords, and 'relocating' them to other countries within the Schengen area. The network of often interconnected document facilitators operates in both sending (Uzbekistan), transit (Turkey and, until 2022, Russia) and host destinations in Europe. Facilitated irregular migration to Europe has become a persistent problem and Eastern European countries have become a major source and transit countries for irregular migrants on their way to Western Europe (Pullat, 2014). Usually up to two thirds of all irregular migration incidents detected by the border guard at all borders within the EU is related to misuse of the visa system, followed by incidents of illegal stay and illegal border crossing (Pullat, 2014). In short, citizens of Uzbekistan obtain short-term Schengen visas, mostly in Tashkent, and travel to Moscow (or sometimes Istanbul/Ankara) to obtain long-term (education, work, residence) visas. However, once these individuals reach their destination countries, which are mostly in Central Europe and the Baltics, they may decide to move on to other Western or Northern European countries in search of better income opportunities.

This research was funded by the Academy of Finland (grant 332192). || An elite as favoring immigrantsIn Excerpt 7, the interviewee is both blaming certain political actors for "gather[ing]" (line 9) immigrants and bringing them to Finland and complaining that Finns have to "provide" (line 8) for these immigrants. The interviewee begins with derogatory references to people associated with origins from the Middle East or Africa (lines 3-6) arriving in Finland. Additionally, throughout Excerpt 7, the interviewee refers to immigrants with the pronoun those (lines 8-12, 14) and implies that immigrants in Finland live on social allowance provided by the Social Insurance Institution (commonly called "Kela" in Finnish, line 15). The interviewee positions the representatives of the political elite as accountable for deliberately having "taken" (line 12) immigrants into Finland.The blame is particularly directed at the Green Party and especially at Pekka Haavisto, Finland's Minister of Foreign Affairs (2019-2023) and a representative of the Green Party. By referring to the elite as "idiots" (line 8) who deliberately "gather" (line 9) or have "taken" (line 12) immigrants into Finland, the interviewee constructs the actions of the elite as senseless while constructing the representatives of the people as being left with no other choice than to "provide" (line 8) for the immigrants. Additionally, the derogatory terms directed at immigrants and the political elite emphasize the agitated position of the interviewee. By stating that "you can't just leave those starving" (line 11), the interviewee further emphasizes the argument that "those shouldn't be taken here at all" (line 12) and "shouldn't be let in at all" (line 15), hence outlining an opposition between the ordinary people and the elite. These discursive strategies serve to construct the populist blame attribution in which the elite is to blame for the problems caused by immigration (Hameleers et al., 2023). Indeed, the interviewee does not construct concern about the well-being of immigrants but rather about the well-being of the Finns, who are allegedly paying the price of the failed integration.The following excerpt further demonstrates how interviewees constructed the alleged wrongdoings of the elite as having negative effects on the lives of the Finnish population.In Excerpt 8, the interviewee complains that Finns are treated unfairly compared to immigrants, contrasting the situation of an imagined Finnish single mother with that of an immigrant mother. The immigrant mother is described as having easy access to welfare benefits, whereas the Finn "struggles" (line 6) with a "teeny-weeny salary" (line 6). This extreme-case formulation (Pomerantz, 1986) functions to highlight this alleged unfairness and construct affective positions between the struggling "us" and more prosperous "them." This excerpt exemplifies the discursive strategy of differentiating the self (Lynn & Lea, 2003), as the interviewee appears to be concerned for the unprivileged while simultaneously arguing against granting social benefits to immigrants. However, it is not the immigrant mothers whose actions have led to this unwanted situation but those of the elite, who determine the provision of social benefits. The elite are portrayed as refusing to give struggling Finns "support from anywhere" (lines 7, 12), which "allows immigrants to get so much more" (lines 17-18). In sum, the presented construction of the elite divides people into Finns who struggle for their living and immigrants who get everything easily (lines 5-7, 12-13; Goodman & Burke, 2011) with the help of the immoral elite (lines 16-18; Hameleers et al., 2023). Hence, this construction serves as a populist attribution of blame (Hameleers et al., 2023), where the actions of the elite have negative outcomes for the Finnish people.In this subsection, we have shown how affective polarization develops out of blaming problems attributed to immigration on Finnish politicians. One construct describes politicians or their legislation as unthinking and holds this thoughtlessness accountable for preventing immigrants' absorption into Finnish society. The other construct, accusing politicians of favoring immigrants to Finns, holds their bias accountable for the hardship facing Finns, mentioning Finns with limited income and especially those expected to draw sympathy from the listener, such as single mothers. This construct differs from the first in positioning only Finns, not immigrants, as victims of failed immigration policies. By attributing responsibility to the elite for challenges connected with immigration, the construct outlines a moral antagonism between ordinary people and the elite. The moral antagonism manifests in concrete form the ingroupoutgroup division associated with the production and reproduction of social identity (Tajfel & Turner, 1979) and qualifies with populist blame attribution (Hameleers et al., 2023). Moral antagonism motivates negativity toward immigrants by constructing them as benefiting unfairly F I G U R E 2 Occurrences, by party preference of interviewees, of subject positions of (a) a system as unthinking or (b) an elite as favoring immigrants in interviewees' talk.from the actions of the elite. In sum, these affective constructs are highly polarizing, as the actions of the "other" are depicted as negatively affecting the welfare of the ingroup consisting of Finnish citizens, who are encouraged to feel negative emotions toward the "other," consisting of politicians in power and their immigrant beneficiaries.Figure 2 presents the distribution of these constructs among the interviewees by their adherence to Finnish political parties. Of particular note is the division between the populist Finns Party and the established parties, as mainly supporters of the Finns Party blamed the elite. || Immigrants as exploitativeThe final discursive construction examined here holds immigrants accountable for unwillingness or inability to integrate into Finnish society. This construct differs from those examined previously in omitting any contrast between two opposing Finnish perspectives on immigration. But these interviewees are like the others in drawing on and reworking blame for discursive purposes. In this construction too, the assignment of blame and reworking of its expression cumulate into affective polarization between a Finnish "us" and an immigrant "them."Excerpt 9 exemplifies talk that positions immigrants as accountable for their failure to integrate into Finnish society. Personality traits, unwillingness, or inability are stated to be at fault (lines 5-6). The interviewee deploys a derogatory term intended to mock refugees seeking asylum-"asylum tourists" (line 2)-that is common in radical-right populist discourse (Sakki & Pettersson, 2016). The term derides refugees as illegitimate and choosing to "abuse" the Finnish society (line 8; Goodman & Speer, 2007) at the cost of Finns and constructs Finns as economically suffering from immoral acts by immigrants (Lynn & Lea, 2003). The interviewee's unconditional terms "lots of," "purely," and "no will whatsoever" (lines 1, 4, 5-6) claim self-evidence for her assertions. By presentation of her assertions as unquestionable, a claim of self-evidence preempts any expression of doubt on the part of her listener (Billig, 1996;Lynn & Lea, 2003). Denial of the opportunity to doubt adds conviction to her representation of immigrants as blameworthy. Her opposition between the homogeneous Finns and immigrants uniformly incapable of integrating echoes far-right political discourse that contrasts "us" and "our" welfare to "them," consisting of parasitic immigrants (Sakki & Pettersson, 2016).In addition to the personal characteristics of immigrants, sometimes their accountability was constructed through reference to their cultural or religious background, as in the following excerpt.Excerpt 10 blames rape on cultural differences between Finns and foreigners. The interviewee begins by assigning self-evidence (lines 8-9; Billig, 1996;Lynn & Lea, 2003) to an assertion that Finnish culture excludes rape. This claim can be considered problematic in light of the Finnish Government's Action Plan for Gender Equality, which places Finnish women as the second most likely to face sexual abuse in the European Union (Ministry of Social Affairs and Health, 2020). The interviewee later continues to claim that foreigners are the committing rapes "because they haven't gotten how one should behave" (lines 11-12). This can be regarded as a way of using liberal arguments to illiberal ends (Augoustinos & Every, 2007), where the liberal tropes of freedom, liberalism, and-in this particular case-women's rights are mobilized to justify discrimination. Further, through culturally essentialist arguments (Verkuyten, 2003), cultural aspects are presented as deeply rooted and thus inevitably incompatible with Finnish or Western culture (lines 6-8). With the use of social categorization and emphasizing the differences between native Finns and immigrants, blame for the failure of integration is thus attributed to these allegedly inherent cultural differences (Goodman & Speer, 2007;Tileaga, 2005). Interestingly, the interviewee's laughter together with the reference to the "legendary discussion" (lines 3-4) on immigrants and rape functions here as a disclaimer, positioning the speaker as informed about negative stereotypes of immigrants yet able to articulate her own reasoned view and to attribute blame to "certain" foreigners (or their cultures) only.This construction positions immigrants as accountable for their unwillingness or inability to immigrate into Finnish society. The construction represents immigrants as intentionally abusing Finland's welfare system and as unfit for Finnish society because of their cultural traits (see Hanson-Easey & Augoustinos, 2012). Other interviewees not quoted here add religion to culture as the obstacle that prevents immigrants from learning to become Finns. In the process, interviewees displaying this construct imply or even assert that Finns suffer from abuses or even crimes committed by immigrants. The contrast of immoral behaviors by the "other" to the innocent "us" is another manifestation of boundary-making separating an ingroup from an outgroup (Tajfel & Turner, 1979), in our interpretation constituting an instance of populist blame attribution aimed at immigrants (Hameleers et al., 2023). Figure 3 shows how the construction of immigrants as accountable varies with adherence to party.

funding_statement: Integrated model of entrepreneur weirdness effects on product creativity and investor funding decisionsIn the preceding sections, we have articulated two pathways through which entrepreneur weirdness may affect product creativity: (a) an entrepreneur creativity path (a positive indirect effect of weirdness on product creativity), and (b) an entrepreneur competence path (a negative indirect effect of weirdness on product creativity). Next, we establish that product creativity affects the actual success of the entrepreneur's pitch. In order to incorporate such practical consequences, we specify the downstream effects on investor funding decisions, in particular the number of bidders (i.e., the number of investors who bid on the product being pitched). The number of bidders has been studied when sellers need to attract potential buyers (e.g., bid competition, Carr, 2005; or in a public bid project, Shrestha & Pradhananga, 2010). A bid or offer generally indicates an investor's decision to fund the pitched idea (typically in return for some equity in the venture). As such, these are critical milestones for entrepreneurs pitching to investors (Boulton et al., 2019;Ciuchta et al., 2018). Since creative products are likely to be valued more by customers (Im et al., 2013) and demonstrate higher market potential (Nakata et al., 2018), we expect product creativity will relate positively to investor funding decisions. On the basis of the aforementioned rationale, we propose the theoretical model depicted in Figure 1, which explains the effects of entrepreneur weirdness on entrepreneurship outcomes (product creativity and investor funding decisions). Our moderation hypotheses, when taken together with the mediation paths shown in Figure 1, imply moderated mediation effects: Hypothesis 4: Entrepreneur warmth moderates the serial indirect effect of entrepreneur weirdness on investor funding decisions via entrepreneur creativity and product creativity, such that the serial indirect effect (i.e., Entrepreneur Weirdness → Entrepreneur Creativity → Product Creativity → Investor Funding Decisions) is more positive when entrepreneur warmth is higher.Hypothesis 5: Entrepreneur warmth moderates the serial indirect effect of entrepreneur weirdness on investor funding decisions via entrepreneur competence and product creativity, such that the serial indirect effect (i.e., Entrepreneur Weirdness → Entrepreneur Competence → Product Creativity → Investor Funding Decisions) is less negative when entrepreneur warmth is higher. || Investor funding decisions.Investor funding decisions (i.e., the number of bidders) was coded by research assistants who were blind to the study hypotheses. For each of the 213 pitches, the first research assistant coded all Sharks who made an offer to each entrepreneur. To test the reliability of this coding, a second coder independently coded a subset of 64 pitches (intercoder reliability r = .97). We utilized the following strategy to count the number of bidders. If there were no offers, we counted it as 0. If the same Shark made several offers, we counted it as 1 (e.g., if one Shark made three offers, it was counted as 1). If more than one Shark was involved in the same bid, we counted the number of Sharks involved in the bid (e.g., if two Sharks offered a joint bid, it was counted as 2). Finally, if the same combination of Sharks made several bids, we counted the number of Sharks involved (e.g., if the same two Sharks offered several bids, it was counted as 2).

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article explored the coming out experiences of South Asian gay and bisexual young men at home.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intersectionality theory suggests that lesbian, gay, and bisexual youth of color may experience double minority stress, due to facing the multiple stressors of sexual minority stigma and racism. Although family support has been identified as important social support for youth, little research has considered how well families support South Asian LGBTQ youth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Semistructured interviews were conducted with 15 gay and bisexual South Asian young men. Data were systematically analyzed according to the principles of interpretive description.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three overarching themes were identified in the analysis including that (a) parents were very concerned about what others would think about their child's sexual orientation; (b) parents demonstrated a wide range of reactions to their child's disclosure, which most commonly included anger, denial, and avoidance; and (c) there are a lack of resources for South Asian sexual minority youth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that because of traditional homophobic attitudes espoused by South Asian cultures, South Asian gay and bisexual youth find it very challenging to navigate coming out to their parents. For the same reasons, it makes it very difficult for South Asian parents to accept their child's sexual orientation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>It is important that interventions to increase parental support of South Asian gay and bisexual youth are culturally relevant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

funding_statement: Contemporary C/MFT training programsSimilar to a national increase in demographic diversity, the C/MFT workforce has experienced a significant increase in cultural diversity over the past decade. The percentage of licensed MFTs who are Black, Indigenous, and/or People of Color (BIPOC) rose from 17% in 2012 to 25% in 2022 (American Association of Marriage and Family Therapy, 2022c). The increase among students was even more pronounced, with 27% of students in MFT programs being BIPOC in 2012, whereas currently, 44% of students in C/MFT programs identify as BIPOC. "Growth was particularly notable among those in the field identifying as Black/African American (up from 4.3% of respondents in 2012 to over 11% of respondents in 2022) and Hispanic, Latino, or Spanish origin (up from 3.77% in 2012 to 7% in 2022)" (MFT Workforce Demographic Report, 2022, p. 4).The American Association of Marriage and Family Therapy (AAMFT), the professional association for C/MFT, has implemented a number of initiatives related separately to diversity and leadership. For example, the AAMFT Minority Fellowship Program, funded by SAMHSA, provides financial support to C/MFT students committed to working with underserved communities (AAMFT, 2022a). The AAMFT Leadership Symposium and Certificate in Leadership program provides training to C/MFTs in areas such as communication, self-awareness, and mentoring (AAMFT, 2022b). However, despite the focus on diversifying the profession and leadership development, conversations about racial justice, power, and the centrality of whiteness as "a pervasive and dominant ideology that is enduring, invisible, and ubiquitous" (Hardy, 2022, p. 9) operating within the C/MFT profession, or as topics of training for leaders, appear to be the subject of little to no AAMFT-initiated systematic undertakings.The larger societal context in which C/MFT programs are embedded is currently characterized by a worldwide response to a once-in-a-century pandemic, increased conversations related to cultural diversity, and rapid advancements in technologies allowing for collaboration among people around the world (Durham, 2022;Khubchandani et al., 2021;WHO, 2021). In early January 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO, 2021) declared a COVID-19 pandemic. Community-wide stay-at-home mandates, followed by state executive orders and policies that eased restrictions on video conferencing and rapidly developed platforms for video conferencing, rapidly expanded the capacity of C/MFT programs nationwide to provide training, therapy, and supervision remotely. At the same time, prolonged periods of social isolation led to increased depression and anxiety among students and faculty (Brown et al., 2021;Woolston, 2020), as well as the general population (Khubchandani et al., 2021).Subsequently, the televised murder of George Floyd in May of 2020 and the release of videos of the killings of Breonna Taylor and Ahmaud Arbery, both of which had occurred earlier in the Spring of 2020, led to an increase in discussions of interpersonal and systemic racism in the national media and among local community activists and policymakers (Pew Research Center, 2021). Estimates suggest over 10,000 demonstrations, nearly 95% involving peaceful protestors protesting police violence, occurred between May 24th and August 22nd, 2020 (ACLED, 2021). Given the focus of C/MFTs on human systems, mental health, and well-being, these societal events and conversations held additional significance for C/MFTs and, thus, translated into expanded tasks, effort, and responsibility for PDs.

coi_statement: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>This paper describes “Turning back the clock” (TBC)—an innovative strategy addressing unacceptable or coercive youth behavior based on nonviolent principles, inspired by the nonviolent resistance movement (NVR)—also called connecting authority or caring authority (CA) approaches to guidance and supervision of parents and other adults. Variants of NVR/CA have been evaluated as effective in RCT and pre–post designs. TBC has not been evaluated regarding its effectiveness but shows promising usability in case studies. The aim of this description of the TBC strategy is to encourage development and testing of its usability on large scale to improve it and pave the way for effectiveness evaluations. The core of TBC is to create possibilities for improving behavior without delay by negotiating the social timeline narrative. This allows improvement through reenactment of events immediately after having said or done something unfortunate or unacceptable instead of waiting for the next comparable situation. Adults introduce the strategy by modeling it before youths are encouraged to improve their own misbehavior immediately without waiting for a later opportunity. Finally, adults declare that a set of unacceptable behaviors will be considered disqualifying to any request or demand, but that attempting again as if it had not happened can be a possibility: Using the TBC strategy. This declaration is intended to increase youth's interest in using TBC themselves, and with successful use reduce escalation of conflicts into coercion and threats.</jats:p>

funding_statement: FundingThe author(s) disclosed receipt of the following financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article: Ramón y Cajal Program awarded to M.B. by the Spanish Ministry of Universities (Grant Number: RYC2021-032887-I). || Grant: RYC2021-032887-I || Perceived Threat as Justification of Restrictive and Inclusive Policies Towards Migrants and Ethnic MinoritiesThe expression of hostility towards an outgroup is only possible within an interpretative framework that delegitimizes them, often portraying outgroup members as enemies (Bar-Tal et al., 2007). Threat, in this context, plays a pivotal role in explaining negative attitudes and hostility towards outgroups (e.g., Stephan et al., 2002Stephan et al., , 2005; see meta-analysis by Riek et al., 2006). Such threat can manifest in different forms, including symbolic threat, which pertains to the perceived endangerment of ingroup cultural norms and values (McConahay, 1986;Sears & Kinder, 1985); realistic threat, which relates to competition for resources such as employment, health, or social services; and even security threats, particularly salient in the context of terrorist attacks. Research has shown that threat is linked to support for the restriction of outgroup members' rights (Carriere et al., 2022;Rapp, 2015;Verkuyten, 2009), including opposition to religious symbols in public spaces ( Van der Noll, 2010). An example illustrating this phenomenon is the case of the mayor of Badalona (Catalonia, Spain) who made the following statement about the Muslim community: "Perhaps it is time for the EU to consider whether it can continue with a policy that gives everyone rights. Not all options are valid". 4  We propose that perceived threat, encompassing both symbolic and realistic dimensions, may underpin the relationship between European attachment and the support for both restrictive and inclusive policies. Existing literature suggests that ingroup identification is highly sensitive to signals that warn about potential harm to the ingroup (Bizman & Yinon, 2001;Verkuyten, 2009), thus indicating a greater propensity to perceive threats, which can intensify intergroup hostility or diminish solidarity with outgroups (Branscombe & Wann, 1994;Tajfel & Turner, 1986;Turner & Reynolds, 2001). Building on this previous evidence, it is plausible to hypothesize that a strong attachment to Europe would be associated with higher perceptions of threat to European community's social cohesion and security. A comprehensive study conducted with large national probabilistic samples from 15 Western European countries found that ingroup identification, perceived threat, and racist attitudes jointly predicted orientations towards migration policies (Jackson et al., 2001). Only one recent study has focused on the role of threat in the link between European attachment and acceptance of immigrants to Europe, suggesting that identification is linked with lower threat, and thus higher acceptance of refugees (Konings et al., 2023). Yet, to our knowledge, no previous research has specifically examined perceived threat among EU citizens and its predictive role in explaining support for restrictive and inclusive policies towards ethnic minorities and immigrants simultaneously.

funding_statement: fair opportunities for poor single mothers in Israel to complete a bachelor's degree.K E Y W O R D S child poverty, higher education, resilient self-efficacy, single mothers, transformative growthThis study examines the sources of empowerment, resilient self-efficacy, and transformative growth of Israeli single mothers in poverty who decided to pursue a BA degree to secure a better future for their children. The National Insurance Institute of Israel (2018) reported that 1.8 million people in Israel live under the poverty line, with 33%, or 842,300, of them being children, and 28.8% being single-parent families with mother heading the family in 94% of cases. Even though this study was conducted in 2017, before COVID-19, the pandemic exacerbated the gender gap in income in Israel and the feminization of poverty (Amir, 2020;Auksanberg, 2020;Goodwin, 2021;Kurlander, 2010).The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) recognizes the intimate connection between serving children's best interest and assisting parents to perform their primary responsibility for the upbringing and development of their children (Art. 27), while ensuring childcare services and facilities for eligible children with working parents (Art. 18). Similarly, among its 17 goals, the UN Sustainable Developmental Goals report (2015) lists achieving a better future by ending poverty in all its forms (Goal 1) and achieving gender equality and empowerment of all women and girls (Goal 5). Given the interlinkages among poverty, gender inequalities, and lack of educational opportunities, this report recommends increasing educational technical and vocational initiatives at all levels to achieve a better future.Drawing from the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and the 2015 United Nations Sustainable Developmental Goals report, education, training, and quality daycare and after-school care services are fundamental targets to empower single mothers to escape poverty and achieve equal opportunities in the job market (Duffee et al., 2016;McLanahan et al., 2014). Studies conducted in the United States and Israel provide evidence that higher education and skill acquisition and training are major long-term solutions to empower single mothers in poverty to achieve economic independence (Armour, 2004;Deprez & Butler, 2001). The Israeli government data indicated that 71% of the single mothers who had graduated with a bachelor's degree had successfully integrated into the job market (Horesh, 2004). Furthermore, up to 70% of poor women participating in work-skills development and training programs operated by feminist organizations such as Shdulat Nashim and Vitzo had successfully gained and sustained employment (Kurlander, 2010).Despite the strong correlation between higher education, job market integration, and economic independence, social services in Israel and the United States seldom facilitate poor single mothers' access to higher education and seldom account for the structural barriers preventing these mothers to complete a degree. Among these barriers are the lack of academic and financial support and lack of low-cost, quality childcare and after-school care alternatives for children (Hobson et al., 2002;Pulkingham et al., 2010).Empowering single mothers in poverty to access higher education and complete a bachelor's degree has been addressed within a Foucauldian perspective. Foucault (1978Foucault ( , 1980) ) argued that power and knowledge join in the top-down dominant discourse of the powerful to produce a body of apparent self-evident truths-knowledge that controls the mind of the oppressed groups and persuades them to participate in their own domination. Furthermore, Nader (1997) emphasized that mind-control mechanisms are also pervasive in Western societies, with experts in psychology, medicine, and social work permeating all realms of social life to restructure the public understanding of "reality" in general, and, for the purposes of the present study, the "truths" about poor single mothers' needs and capabilities, thus reducing to silence single mothers' preferences, objections, and whatever is left of their resistance (Geiger, 2002). Foucault (1980) nevertheless explained that in all systems of domination and subjugation, the subjugated others are not totally powerless: "As soon as there is a relation of power, there is a possibility of resistance" (p. 13). Working "offstage" at the micro-social level and from the bottom up, those who are seemingly powerless produce "hidden transcripts" of resistance that reveal the contradictions in the dominant discourse and other ways of understanding of their reality (Foucault, 1983). Bandura (1986) also argued that individuals are far from being passive victims even in a potentially controlling and oppressive environment that seems to determine their destiny, such as welfare and poverty. Cognitive processes such as self-efficacy perception, empowerment, the ability to exercise agency, and successful actions in such an environment influence each other in a process of reciprocal determinism. Agency refers to a person's actions that will generate self-efficacy perception or empowerment (Bandura, 1986). Perceived self-efficacy refers to a individuals' beliefs in their ability to influence events that affect their life. Resilient self-efficacy perception develops in the process of overcoming obstacles and successfully exercising agency in controlling and threatening situations. Reciprocally, resilient self-efficacy perception diminishes the sense of vulnerability, enhances motivation, and triggers the cognitive resources to exercise agency, which ultimately results in the adoption of efficient and successful strategies of action in a hazardous or oppressive environment (Bandura & Adams, 1977). Herbst (2012) and Herbst andBenjamin (2012) applied Foucault's (1983) theory of power and knowledge to demonstrate two opposite dominant discourses that have emerged in Israel before and after the 2003 welfare reform and have controlled public understanding by defined and redefined "truths" about single mothers in poverty. Before 2003, single mothers in Israel were celebrated in the public discourse as Jewish mothers who gave birth and raised future soldiers who would defend their country (Berkovitch, 2001). Hence, the Single Parent Family Law (1992) entitled single mothers, in their role as caretaker, to receive financial assistance from the state.The 2003 Omnibus Welfare reform in Israel that significantly reduced child support allowances and social services for single mothers paralleled the 1994 "Welfare to Work" reform in the United States. The neo-liberal ideology of individual self-sufficiency and economic independence on which these reforms were based resulted in redefinition poor single mothers in the dominant discourse. These new truths presented single mothers as lacking autonomy, unable to earn a living, and exploiting the taxpayer's money (Doron, 2003;Paz-Fuchs, 2004). Consequently, the 2003 reforms were inevitable decrees "rescuing" these mothers from their dependency on the state while pushing them to find employment and become economically independent (Herbst & Benjamin, 2012;Millar, 2005;Millar & Ridge, 2008;Skevik, 2005). The only single mothers exempt from such decrees were those with children less than 2 years of age. These "truths" about single mothers obviously ignored the reality single mothers face as they continued to take care of their children and could only be employed part time (Hobson et al., 2002;Pulkingham et al., 2010). Part-time employment in an unskilled job, lack of daycare facilities, and the sharp decrease in allowances did little to empower single mothers in poverty to achieve economic independence (Dodson, 2007;Naon et al., 2010).Several antipoverty programs in the United States, grasping the strong correlation between higher education and financial independence, have provided financial assistance to single mothers to enable them to pursue a college degree. However, they often failed to recognize the priority of children's needs in a single mother's life, and the lack of quality daycare or after-school educational alternatives often results in single mothers dropping out of college (Chase-Lansdale & Brooks-Gunn, 2014;Edin & Kefalas, 2005;King et al., 2011).Recognizing the centrality of children's needs, well-being, and prospects as prime incentives motivating single mothers to complete a college degree, several researchers (Freeman, 2017;Hill et al., 2007;Holyfield, 2002) have recommended a two-generation approach to empowering poor single mothers to pursue an education while providing a quality educational environment for their children. The few second-wave antipoverty programs in the United States that have implemented this approach have enabled mothers to graduate and successfully enter the job market (Duffee et al., 2016;McLanahan et al., 2014).In Israel, antipoverty programs enabling single mothers to pursue a degree seldom exist, and social services policies have created serious obstacles preventing single mothers to access higher education. Before 2008, college enrollment for single mothers in poverty entailed giving up child support, and mothers who resisted this draconian decree had to report fraudulently to the Social or Unemployment Services that they neither worked nor studied. As of July 22, 2008, these policies have been somewhat modified, and single mothers are entitled to pursue a degree without losing child support under the conditions that (a) they had been receiving benefits for 16 months before college enrollment, (b) study at least 36 hours a week, and (c) completed a degree within the 3-year period during which students in Israel matriculate. These requirements have often discouraged single mothers from enrolling due to their multiple responsibilities of childcare, work, and study combined with the inability to extend their studies beyond 3-year requirement (Kurlander, 2010).The Katzir program, funded by the Rashi Foundation, a nonprofit Israeli organization, is, to the researcher's best knowledge, the only program that gives single mothers in poverty the opportunity to pursue a college degree when providing them with financial assistance and wraparound services. Fifteen single mothers are selected for this program each year and receive a full tuition waiver annually, a monthly stipend of 500 NIS (approximately 120 US dollars), as well as tutoring, individual and group counseling, and crisis intervention. Program participation remains confidential, a fact that was very much appreciated by the program participants. "No one knows that I am in this program unless I tell them. I am just like anyone else. There is no difference between me and other students in class" (Meyrav, 11 years 1 ). However, like the firstwave antipoverty programs in the United States, children's needs for daycare and alternative after-school programs have been ignored. Patton (2002) rightly argued that to judge the effectiveness of programs and services, "it can be as important to understand the stories behind the numbers as to have the statistics themselves" (p. 152). In this light, my research efforts concentrated on those invisible but most important actors of the Katzir program: poor single mothers and their experience when pursuing a degree. My goals were (a) to determine the sources of empowerment and resilient self-efficacy that motivated single mothers to access higher education and complete a degree while overcoming crises and obstacles and (b) to examine the transformative growth mothers and children experienced in the process of acquiring knowledge and completing a degree.

Despite their ability to correctly recall both positive and negative components of the stories, children in both cultures often agreed to only one emotion and rarely agreed to both. This finding is consistent with previous research with Western children (Donaldson & Westerman, 1986;Harris, 1983;M. Peng et al., 1992). It supports the idea that recognizing the co-occurrence of mixed emotions poses a widespread challenge for children under the age of 10. A plausible interpretation of that challenge is that even when children have encoded both the negative and positive aspects of a situation, their pre-existing ideas about the compatibility of positive and negative emotions guide their appraisal of that situation. Children who think that such emotions cannot co-exist tend to appraise the emotional implications of only one of the two story components, whereas children who think that such emotions can co-exist tend to engage in a more thorough appraisal-to appraise the emotional implications of both components rather than just one. This interpretation is consistent with the link found in both cultures between children's answer to the final general question about mixed emotions and the frequency with which they agreed to both emotions. It is also consistent with earlier research showing that younger children are more likely to acknowledge both emotions if they are first prompted by an adult to appraise the emotional implications of each of the two story components before being asked about the possibility of mixed emotions (M. Peng et al., 1992).Moreover, children in both cultures tended to think about and justify their ideas about mixed emotions in a similar way. At the end of the interview, children were explicitly asked whether they could feel both happy and sad at the same time. In both cultures, around 60% of children said "yes." Among children who said "yes," around 80% of the children in both cultures offered an example and around 80% of their examples could indeed elicit positive and negative emotions simultaneously. This suggests that when children in both cultures agreed to the idea of mixed emotions, their agreement was based on a similar conceptualization and recourse to similarly appropriate examples.Previous research has found that children's acknowledgment of mixed emotions increases with age (Donaldson & Westerman, 1986;Harris, 1983;Harter & Buddin, 1987). Consistent with previous research, we found that older children were more likely to say "yes" than younger children to the final general question of whether they could feel both happy and sad at the same time. However, we did not find an age effect children's agreement to both emotions when answering questions about the four stories. It should be noted, however, that previous research included children at and over the age of 10 and showed that children under the age of 10 often have difficulty in acknowledging mixed emotions (Donaldson & Westerman, 1986;Harris, 1983;Harter & Buddin, 1987). In comparison, the current study only included children up to the age of 9, which may explain the absence of age effect for children's agreement to both emotions for the stories. Thus, it is plausible that older children in the current study were beginning to understand the idea of mixed emotions and could often acknowledge mixed emotions when asked explicitly (as in the final general question), but often failed to appraise the emotional implications of each story component, particularly since they were not prompted to do so (M. Peng et al., 1992).

coi_statement: Disclosure statementNo potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s). || Self-disclosureThe concept of self-disclosure is defined as the behavior of sharing private personal information with others (Altman & Taylor, 1973;Lee et al., 2020). Studies related to self-disclosure are important for psychotherapy and counseling. Jourard and Lasakow (1958) and Cozby (1973) considered self-disclosure an indicator of mental health, an effect in interpersonal relationships, and a cause or solution of mental health. Therefore, in most areas of counseling, self-disclosure by counselees is crucial for solving problems.Several studies have been conducted on the interaction of CA and the self-disclosure of participants. The research began with the CASA paradigm, presupposing the claim that a machine's social presence can be triggered when it represents human characteristics in visual elements, voice, and language (Nass & Moon, 2000). Heckman and Wobbrock (2000) and Moon (2000) found that anthropomorphic chatbots can improve the sense of trust of users.Furthermore, applying anthropomorphic conditions to the conversation scripts of the chatbot can positively entice participants to self-disclose.For health-related information in particular, people prefer chatbots over telephone services because they believe that chatbots guarantee anonymity (Crutzen et al., 2011). People believe that the personal information they disclose will not be leaked to the world because of the perception that chatbots will keep secrets (Lee et al., 2020). However, some previous studies have found that agent credibility and participant self-disclosure may decrease in the presence of anthropomorphic interactions between agent and participant (Bailenson et al., 2006;Kim et al., 2018). In counseling situations, as the characteristics of the counselor contribute significantly to the counseling outcome, it is necessary to understand the correlation between the anthropomorphism of the chatbot and the self-disclosure of the counselee.Therefore, we set the degree of participant self-disclosure according to the anthropomorphic characteristics of the chatbot as a dependent variable and used it as an indicator to predict the effect of the counseling chatbot. || Self-disclosureIn this study, we measured the degree of self-disclosure as a key metric for identifying the results of the interaction   with the counseling chatbot. We adopted the revised selfdisclosure scale (RSDS) proposed by Wheeless (1976), who developed the RSDS to measure self-disclosure in four dimensions: control of depth, honesty, amount, and valence of disclosure. However, we only used the control of depth and honesty of disclosure among the four dimensions as performance metrics because linguistic interactions in counseling play an important role in determining the counseling quality. || Honesty of disclosureWhen the participants talked to the chatbot with a visual interface cue, their honesty of self-disclosure decreased (F ¼ 4.547, p ¼ 0.036 < 0.05, M ¼ 5.47, SD ¼ 0.93). This implies that the presence of a visual interface cue adversely affects the honest attitudes of the participants in the counseling process (see Tables 6, 7). The interaction test results revealed that the interaction effect of the personality and visual interface cues of the chatbot (F ¼ 5.198, p ¼ 0.025 < 0.05) and the interaction effect of the gender, personality, and visual interface cues of the chatbot (F ¼ 4.965, p ¼ 0.028 < 0.05) were statistically significant. Per the individual t-test results, the degree of honesty with and without visual interface cues exhibited a significant difference when the personality of the chatbot was introverted (t ¼ 2.67, p ¼ 0.010) (see Table 8), but showed no significant difference when the chatbot was extroverted (t ¼ À0.14, p ¼ 0.891). When the visual interface cue was provided under the introvert condition, the honesty of the participants decreased; however, there was no significant change in the extrovert condition. Here, the difference in honesty with and without visual interface cues was larger for the female chatbot than that for the male chatbot (see Figure 3). For example, when the visual interface cue was provided for the male chatbot, honesty decreased under the introvert and extrovert conditions. In the case of the female chatbot, when the visual interface cue was provided, honesty significantly decreased in the introverted personality and increased in the extroverted personality. Therefore, the design strategy when creating anthropomorphic characteristics should change depending on the gender of the chatbot. The interaction effect of the genders of the chatbot and participant (F ¼ 6.273, p ¼ 0.014 < 0.05) and the interaction effect of the genders of the agent, participant, and anthropomorphic interface (F ¼ 6.050, p ¼ 0.016 < 0.05) were   statistically significant (see Table 6). In the case of female participants, the honesty of self-disclosure was lower when the chatbot was female than when it was male; in contrast, it increased in the case of male participants. Here, the difference based on the gender of the chatbot was greater when the visual interface cue was provided than when it was not (see Figure 4). As a disordinal interaction effect, it can be interpreted that when a chatbot of the opposite gender to the participant is provided, the honesty of self-disclosure increases; when a visual interface cue is provided, the effect enhances further. || Control of depth of disclosureThe two-way interaction effect of the genders of the chatbot and participant (F ¼ 6.962, p ¼ 0.01 < 0.05) was statistically significant (see Table 6). Per the individual t-test, when the participant was male (t ¼ À0.79, p ¼ 0.434), there was no significant difference in the control of depth between the genders of the chatbots; however, when the participant was female (t ¼ 3.12, p ¼ 0.003), the difference was significant (see Table 9). In the case of female participants, the control of depth was lower when the chatbot was female than when it was male, and it was higher in the case of male participants (see Figure 5). Therefore, when a chatbot of the opposite gender to the participant is provided, the control of depth of disclosure increases.

funding_statement: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a known risk of combat for those in the military. Prevalence amongst combat soldiers is around 12% with this figure seen in Western (Hines et al., 2014) and Israeli (Solomon et al., 2012) militaries. This prevalence is predominantly studied amongst veterans deployed to battlefronts such as Iraq and Afghanistan and either upon return from a specific front or in a treatment-seeking population. The current study was designed to assess the prevalence of PTSD and associated mental health symptoms amongst combat and non-combat veterans in the Israeli military; where combat exposure is not as a result of deployment overseas and where no comparison data currently exists. Military units in Israel are designated as combat (e.g. front line infantry, parachute and tank units), combat support (e.g. medical or logistics units) or non-combat (e.g. intelligence, office-based and spokesperson units) and this determines economic and social support during and following service (Kol Zchut, 2023). Combat soldiers are Correspondence should be addressed to Anna Harwood-Gross, METIV Israel Psychotrauma Center, Herzog Medical Center, Jerusalem, Israel. (E-mail: anna@metiv.org).With gratitude to Alon Weltman and Roni Meisels from METIV who helped with the conceptualization of the study. The research was funded by METIV Israel Psychotrauma Center. This research received no specific grant from any funding agency, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.DB conceived the study and edited protocol and manuscript. AHG was involved in conception and designed, analysed and interpreted data and wrote the study. NS was involved in data collection, analysis and writing the study. highly regarded and their ongoing exposure to potentially traumatic and life-threatening situations causes them to be referred to as the "most important element of the military" (Gantz & Tzur, 2017).There is limited research into modern-day militaries serving in battlefronts close to home, but there is emerging evidence that they may have different vulnerabilities and potential for distress. In comparisons of mental health outcomes for veterans of the UK military, (when the majority, over 60%, had been deployed to Northern Ireland), there was a disproportionate representation of residents of Northern Ireland seeking treatment for mental health problems (compared to residents of England, Scotland and Wales who served away from their home residence) (Murphy et al., 2019). Additionally, veterans from Northern Ireland displayed greater health difficulties with longer times between discharge and turning to help (Ashwick & Murphy, 2018) though this was studied in a treatment-seeking sample. In a recent, (non-treatment-seeking sample) survey of 1267 Northern Irish veterans of the UK Armed Forces, far greater numbers of service members who served on home territory had PTSD and other psychological difficulties compared to those who served overseas (Armour et al., 2021). Ongoing threat and the complex societal-political interplay of living in or adjacent to the battlefield has been indicated to contribute to the higher levels of PTSD and complex PTSD in these populations (Spikol et al., 2022).In militaries which serve predominantly on home territory, as outlined by the preliminary work above (Armour et al., 2021), veterans are subjected to ongoing threats and trauma reminders which may exacerbate trauma-associated symptoms and these are present whether deployed to the delineated battlefield or in a non-combat, non-battlefield position. This makes comparison to existing literature on combat and non-combat veterans difficult and complicates an already varied field.Delineating the definition of a combat and non-combat soldier is complex and the majority of the research comparing these two occupational definitions is predominantly on deployed soldiers from the USA. In a key meta-analysis (Hines et al., 2014) and epidemiological study (Donoho et al., 2017) which included thousands of participants, the complexity is apparent. These two studies compared combatants and non-combatants deployed to war zones (Iraq or Afghanistan) far from their home soil (Netherlands, USA and UK; Hines et al., 2014 and USA;Donoho et al., 2017) and thus were inherently propelled into a combat zone even if not employed as a combatant (e.g. a truck driver deployed to Afghanistan would be categorised as a non-combatant though would experience deployment to a combat zone). The definition of non-combatant in the above studies is loose and included peace-keeping corps whose military identity and training is combat related though they are on non-combat missions and in Donoho and colleagues' study, considered a non-combatant if they were not exposed to combat (Donoho et al., 2017).In the Israeli military, there is a clear delineation of combatant and non-combatant soldiers though given the home nature of the battlefield, both may experience exposure to combat. Combatants are soldiers who were trained for the battlefield. During their military service, they engage both in home-ground combat situations and on or across border battlefronts. Non-combatants are soldiers who were neither trained for combat (undergoing brief, non-specific training) nor assigned to it. They include intelligence officers, non-combatant professionals (such as lawyers, social workers and trainers) and logistics positions. Nonetheless, due to the nature of the Israeli military battleground, both combatants and non-combatants can be exposed to combat experiences (such as gunfire, base infiltration and targeting based on uniformed identification).As the studies above outline, in war zones, non-combatants are not immune from combat exposure (indeed, it appears the act of deployment in militaries where they are predominantly fighting overseas, provides exposure to combat events for all branches of the military). Additionally, those who experience combat exposure are at a greater risk of developing PTSD regardless of combatant status. Furthermore, the studies outlined above frequently attest that veteran care is often biased towards combat veterans with assessment and funding boards impacted by occupation in the military. This is evident upon return to civilian life but also in resilience and de-briefing offered immediately upon return from war zones to combatants as opposed to non-combatants (Adler, Castro, & McGurk, 2009).As far as the authors are aware, no study comparing combatant and non-combatant levels of PTSD and associated symptomologies with veterans of the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF). In Israel, PTSD amongst the general population fluctuates, though at times of increased conflict can be as high as 10% (Gidron et al., 2004). Despite the high rate of military service in the Israeli population due to mandatory service (around 50% of potential recruits draft each year according to statistics released annually by the Ministry of Defense), there have been few studies comparing military-related outcomes amongst combatants and non-combatants following their compulsory military service. Indeed a 2015 study on risky behaviour was the only published study identified comparing combat and non-combat IDF veterans (Garyn-Tal & Shahrabani, 2015). Amongst treatment-seeking populations, Levi and Lubin demonstrated that following the Lebanon war in 2006 and the Gaza operation in 2009 respectively, more combat soldiers (59.8% and 72%) than non-combat soldiers in combat support roles (37.5% and 43%) sought treatment for PTSD (Levi & Lubin, 2018) but as outlined above, there may many reasons why combatants are more likely than non-combatants to seek help from the Ministry of Defence or IDF official PTSD clinics. Indeed, Levi and Lubin sampled combatants and combat-support soldiers indicating that non-combatants who were not in support-combat roles were not included in the study or did not seek treatment.The current study was designed to compare and contrast rates of PTSD and associated symptom profiles (depression, anxiety, somatic and aggressiveness) amongst IDF combat and non-combat veterans in a non-treatment-seeking sample. It has been frequently reported that veterans are at increased risk of mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, aggression and a range of somatic symptoms not necessarily related to the physical strains of service (Macmanus et al., 2014;Thompson et al., 2015). The connection between PTSD and unexplained somatic symptoms is now included in the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines for the identification of PTSD (National Institute426 HARWOOD-GROSS, STERN, BROMfor Health and Care Excellence, 2018) and physical symptoms such as chronic pain have been demonstrated at higher rates in veteran populations and may precede depression or anxiety diagnoses (Thompson et al., 2015).It was predicted, that compared to veterans from non-combat roles, due to the ongoing combatant nature of their position, combat veterans would have higher levels of PTSD, depression, anxiety, somatic and aggression symptoms. As this was an exploratory study, with no such information previously collated from a military not deploying overseas, it was hypothesized that this may be due to higher levels of combat exposure and thus combat exposure was included in comparisons as a potentially more significant grouping variable.

coi_statement: The disclosure-liking effects in human-machine interactionThe disclosure-liking effects were widely examined in the context of human-machine interaction. In the 1990s, Nass et al. (1994Nass et al. ( , 1996) ) proposed the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) Paradigm. This paradigm posited that humans socially perceive, interact, and respond to machines automatically and mindlessly despite the key differences between humans and machines. In this line of research, Moon (2000) examined the dynamics associated with soliciting intimate information from consumers via computers and found that consumers' S-D tendencies were consistent with the norms of reciprocity and social propriety in the HHI context. A computer that disclosed some information about itself was more likely to lead participants to reveal intimate information about themselves and become attracted to it; as a result, they responded more positively to the products recommended by the computer.Recent research has continued to document evidence in the human-machine interaction context, expanding the territory from computers to AI and the Internet of Things. However, these studies have provided sporadic evidence confirming or disconfirming the disclosure-liking effects (see summary in Table 1). First, much recent evidence supported the intimacy ! liking effect. For instance, in conversations with a supposed chatbot or person, the emotional outcomes (i.e., feeling better and reduced negative mood), relational outcomes (i.e., perceived partner warmth and enjoyment of conversation), and psychological outcomes (i.e., liking of partner and self-affirmation) were observed to be equivalent, independent of the type of S-D the individuals engaged in (Ho et al., 2018). In addition, once people engaged in intimate S-D with conversational agents, a reversed self-serving attribution bias appeared. People did not take personal responsibility for dyadic success or blame the agents for dyadic failure in human-agent dyadic tasks (Li & Rau, 2019).In addition, the findings have been more mixed regarding receiving S-D from a machine. In a human-robot collaboration experiment, people felt less in control but liked the robot more when the robot disclosed its affective state. Conversely, providing people with the ability to control robot S-D increased their sense of control but decreased their liking for the robot (Siino et al., 2008). Nomura and Kawakami (2011) conducted an experiment to compare the conditions of no S-D, positive S-D, and negative S-D from a small humanoid robot; and found that the subjects' anxiety toward the robot's communication capacity was stable before and after receiving positive S-D from the robot, while their anxiety increased in the other two conditions. A more recent experiment by Ling and Bj€ orling (2020) examined how three types of robot disclosure (emotional, technical, and by-proxy) affected robot perception and human disclosure behavior during a stress-sharing activity. The findings suggested that emotional robot disclosure resulted in the lowest perceived robot safety.Lastly, the evidence is relatively scarce regarding the reciprocity ! liking effect involving both human S-D to machine and machine S-D to human. For instance, Eyssel et al. (2017) found that S-D to the robot or receiving S-D from the robot did not affect participants' perceptions, such as likability and perceived interaction quality with the robot. On the contrary, Meng and Dai (2021) found that after the human participant disclosed to the AI, the AI chatbot's reciprocal S-D enhanced the positive effect of emotional support on worry reduction. || Disclosure statementNo potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).

coi_statement: Desire to learn about the disclosure statementAs shown in Figure 6, out of 120 participants who were shown the disclosure statement during the persuasive attack, only 28.4% stated that they would want to learn how persuasive features may impact their gambling behavior. There was no significant difference in desire to learn based on gender, PGSI group or inoculation condition at Phase 2.Participants who were asked how likely they were to click the "learn more" button were also asked to give a rationale for their answers. Figure 7 illustrates the rationale provided by the participants for their decision to either engage or not engage with the disclosure statement (i.e., explainable persuasion).Participants who stated that they would like to learn more about how persuasive features may impact their gambling behavior indicated that providing such explanations will show the integrity of the gambling operators and give players control over their gambling decisions. One participant stated that such information could be especially beneficial when players are chasing losses, as interacting with the information can disrupt such harmful behavior. Participants who said they would not learn more about how persuasive features may impact their gambling behavior indicated they would not be interested in such information. This lack of interest was due to prior knowledge of the persuasive techniques employed by gambling operators, denial of gambling problems, immersion in gambling, desensitization to system warnings in general, and disinterest in the pop-up online casino bonus offer used in the study. Some participants expressed mistrust in gambling operators, claiming that such information will be "superficial" and offered just to comply with regulations. Several participants indicated concerns regarding the presentation of the disclosure statement.Participants claimed that the disclosure statement was difficult to read due to fine print and lengthy wording, neither of which encourage responsible gambling behavior. || Disclosure statementNo potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).

In turn, people's relative comparisons may negatively impact well-being (Osborne et al., 2015;Schneider, 2019). Indeed, feelings of relative deprivation-stemming from subjective feelings of disadvantage-predict myriad individual and social outcomes above and beyond one's objective position in society (Smith et al., 2012). Notably, individuals can either feel deprived relative to other individuals (individual-based relative deprivation [IRD]) or that their group is deprived relative to other groups (group-based relative deprivation [GRD]), provided they appraise themselves or their group as unfairly disadvantaged (Runciman, 1966). While feelings of GRD (relative to IRD) more strongly predict group-based outcomes like collective action (Abrams & Grant, 2012), IRD (relative to GRD) more strongly predicts individual-level outcomes including lower self-esteem (Walker, 1999). Thus, how one perceives their income relative to other individuals may help explain how income affects well-being (Buttrick & Oishi, 2017).Considerable work illustrates the impact of objective markers of relative income on well-being (for a review, see Clark & D'Ambrosio, 2015). For example, cross-sectional research demonstrates that the negative relationship between relative income and life satisfaction is stronger in nations with higher levels of income inequality (i.e., countries with more salient differences between the "haves" and the "have-nots"; see Cheung & Lucas, 2016). Experimental (Card et al., 2012) and panel (Luttmer, 2005) data further show that one's income relative to others dramatically impacts well-being.Though informative, the extant literature has predominantly focused on aggregate measures of income inequality or material comparisons of individuals' income to others in the local community (see Smith et al., 2012, for discussion). However, relative deprivation theory posits that individuals must perceive themselves as unfairly disadvantaged to feel relatively deprived. Accordingly, studies that measure one's perceptions of-and affective responses to-their societal position reveal stronger associations with well-being than do studies that just assess objective conditions (Smith et al., 2012). Thus, examining people's perceptions of their position relative to similar others is needed to understand the psychological mechanisms underlying income's effects on well-being (Osborne et al., 2015).

funding_statement: Attachment and prosocialityEarly interactions with caregivers established individuals' internal attachment representations (Bowlby, 1982). Children likely develop a secure attachment style if they get consistent and warm responses from caregivers in times of need. In contrast, they likely develop an insecure attachment style if they usually get inconsistent Correspondence should be addressed to Lili Wu, CAS Key Laboratory of Mental Health, Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, No. 16, Lincui Road, Beijing 100101, China. (E-mail: wull@psych.ac.cn) This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant No. 31871125). WB and WL conceived and designed the experiments, analysed the data, and wrote the manuscript. WB performed the experiments. PX, JM and ZJ revised the manuscripts. All authors contributed to the article and approved the submitted version. and cold responses from caregivers (Bowlby, 1982). For adults, individual differences in attachment style can be mapped on two dimensions-attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance (Brennan et al., 1998). Attachment anxiety refers to the worries about a relationship partner's availability and supportiveness in times of need, while attachment avoidance refers to the discomfort with dependency and distrust in a relationship partner's goodwill and capacity to help (Brennan et al., 1998). People who score low in both dimensions are supposed to be the securely attached ones.Attachment security priming momentarily enhances people's sense of security, thereby enabling them to think and behave in a manner that can be characterised as securely attached people (Gillath et al., 2022). The enhanced sense of security would affect subsequent mental and behavioural outcomes, including prosocial feelings and behaviours (Mikulincer & Shaver, 2020).Previous research emphasised the effect of specific positive factors between attachment security and prosociality (i.e., empathy, Gillath et al., 2005;Mikulincer & Shaver, 2005). A recent meta-analysis showed that negative or antisocial factors have medium predictive effects on prosocial behaviour, which is comparable to the predictive effect of positive factors (e.g., empathy) (Thielmann et al., 2020). Therefore, the present study extended previous research by examining the mediating roles of a negative factor, that is, moral disengagement.
